The faint marks visible are not intentional writing, but **bleed-through** (also called show-through), where ink from the writing on the other side of the page has seeped through the fibers over time.</note>

# Theophrastus Paracelsus
# The Volume Beyond Wonders and The Work Beyond Wonders
<note>original: "Volumen Paramirum und Opus Paramirum". These are two of the most significant medical-philosophical treatises by Paracelsus. The term <term>Paramirum</term> (derived from the Greek 'para'—beyond—and Latin 'mirum'—wonder) refers to his theory of the five hidden causes of disease that exist beyond the mere physical symptoms known to traditional medicine.</note>

->Edited, introduced,<-
->and with notes by<-
->Dr. Franz Strunz<-
<note>Franz Strunz (1875–1953) was an influential Austrian historian of science and a pioneer in the modern study of Paracelsus, helping to reframe him as a serious philosopher and scientist rather than just a folk hero or magician.</note>

## The City of Paracelsus
## Salzburg

<note>original: "Der Paracelsus-Stadt Salzburg". Paracelsus was deeply connected to Salzburg, having sought refuge there under the protection of the Prince-Archbishop late in his life. He died in the city in 1541, and his tomb remains a site of pilgrimage in the St. Sebastian Cemetery.</note>

## Preface

<insert>A</insert>S will be discussed in more detail in the introduction, the editing of these two famous writings by Hohenheim <note>Paracelsus's birth name was Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541).</note> followed the general outlines of the Huser text of the Basel Quarto Edition [1589–1591] as a template. <note>Johannes Huser was a physician who, decades after Paracelsus’s death, collected and edited his scattered manuscripts into a definitive ten-volume edition.</note> The need has made itself felt—and this applies to the two *Paramirum* writings <note>The *Paramirum* works (specifically the *Opus Paramirum* and *Volumen Paramirum*) are foundational texts where Paracelsus explains that diseases are not just physical imbalances, but arise from five "spheres" or influences.</note> quite differently than to the *Paragranum* <note>The *Paragranum* is another of Paracelsus's major works, defining the "four pillars" of medicine: philosophy, astronomy, alchemy, and ethics.</note>—to correct the text, which in places was severely distorted and made ambiguous by printing errors or disruptive abbreviations, primarily insofar as fluid readability requires it. Doing any kind of violence to the text was far from our minds, especially the intention of offering a modernized "translation." Paracelsus cannot be "translated" without destroying the unique, antique timbre of his linguistic tone. The original spelling was—so long as it did not hinder readability or obscure the meaning of the words—largely left unchanged, a circumstance that makes it clear that a strictly consistent orthography <note>standardized spelling</note> could not be maintained. Fundamental guiding principles have been highlighted by me through **spaced type**. <note>The original German uses "Sperrdruck," a typographic style of emphasis where spaces are placed between letters; this translation uses bold to reflect that intended emphasis.</note> The annotations refer only to important questions and are, of course, not intended to be exhaustive.

I find myself obligated to [thank] the highly esteemed library—

<summary>In this preface, the editor explains the decision to use Johannes Huser’s late 16th-century edition as a primary source while correcting historical printing errors to improve readability for modern readers. The editor emphasizes preserving Paracelsus's original linguistic style and "timbre" rather than providing a modernized paraphrase.</summary>
<keywords>Johannes Huser, Basel Quarto Edition, Paramirum, Paragranum, Hohenheim, linguistics, editorial method, orthography, medical history</keywords>

# Introduction

<insert>
**T**
</insert>HIS present new edition of the *Volume* [*First Paramirum*] and the *Work* [*Second Paramirum*] <note>The title *Paramirum* is a term coined by Paracelsus, roughly meaning "Beyond Wonder" or "About Miraculous Things." It refers to his system of medicine that looked beyond traditional medieval theories.</note> is based in its fundamental features on the excellent Huser text of the Basel quarto edition [1589–1591] <note>Johannes Huser (c. 1545–1600) was a physician who spent years collecting Paracelsus’s original manuscripts to create the first definitive printed collection of his works.</note>. Urgent textual changes for the sake of easier readability and corrections of disruptive printing errors have been attempted. The most essential annotations are intended to bring the understanding of the often alien content closer to the reader. Guiding principles have been highlighted through *spaced lettering* <note>original: *Sperrdruck*, a German typesetting tradition where characters are spaced out to provide emphasis, similar to italics.</note>. Both works are found in the first part of the aforementioned edition¹), specifically the *Volume*²) *of the Medical Paramirum of Theophrastus, On Medical Diligence* on pages 1–64, and the *Work*³) *Paramirum . . . Made in Honor of the Venerable . . . Joachim von Wadt* <note>Joachim von Wadt (1484–1551), also known as Vadianus, was a Swiss humanist, physician, and reformer who was a contemporary of Paracelsus.</note> on pages 67–140. What interests us now above all are the questions: When did these *Paramira* originate, or rather, what other printed editions are known besides the one mentioned above? We know that in December 1529, Paracelsus was on his way toward Regensburg—his time in Nuremberg was already behind him—and he interrupted his journey in the solitude of Beratzhausen in the Laber Valley. Here the *Volumen Paramirum* and the *Paragranum* <note>The *Paragranum* (meaning "Beyond the Grain") is another of Paracelsus's foundational works where he describes the four pillars of medicine: Philosophy, Astronomy, Alchemy, and Virtue.</note> [were written]. The *Volumen*, also called the *First Paramirum*, appeared in its first and only separate edition in the year 1575: 

->**THE VOLUME OF MEDICINE PARAMIRUM BY PHILIPPUS THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS, the highly experienced German Philosopher and Doctor of both Medicines <note>This title indicates a physician qualified in both "Physic" (internal medicine) and "Surgery."</note>. On medical diligence, Concerning the skill of the physician. Never before released in print. With Imperial privilege. Printed in Strasbourg by Christian Müller. 1575.** 8º. 8 leaves + 141 numbered pages + 5 unnumbered pages.<-

The *Opus*, called the *Second Paramirum*, dates to his time in St. Gallen [1531]. It was published as early as 1562—thus earlier than the *Volumen*: 

->**The Book PARAMIRUM, of the Honorable and Highly Experienced AUREOLUS THEOPHRASTUS von Hohenheim, in which the true causes of diseases and complete cures are briefly explained; useful and necessary for all physicians. With an attached JUDGMENT, excellent**<-

❦ Both of the *Paramirum* writings <note>The word "Paramirum" was coined by Paracelsus, likely meaning "Beyond Wonder" or "Concerning Miracles."</note> constitute one of Hohenheim’s <note>The family name of the physician better known as Paracelsus.</note> most famous and personal works. While the *Book Paragranum* <note>The "Book of the Four Pillars" of medicine.</note> was the — albeit polemically <note>Refers to a strong verbal or written attack; argumentative.</note> colored — exposition of the guidelines for the new scientific and medical method, the *Volume* <note>original: "Volumen"</note> and *Work Beyond Wonder* <note>original: "Opus Paramirum"</note> together provide us with almost everything that is of significance regarding his “teachings.” Almost all questions of natural research, medicine, and philosophy that ever occupied him are addressed here; some in detailed discussion, some only briefly and suggestively, and some in a version that we then encounter reworked in other writings. Both *Paramirum* writings contain the most essential components of Hohenheim’s system. This is true first because an attempt is made here to work out a synthesis in broad strokes and with deliberate emphasis, and secondly because the flowing prose is not burdened by obstructive polemics. These two works specifically show Hohenheim’s unique character as a natural researcher, physician, and philosopher best, even if his theological side recedes more into the background. Everything here pushes to the surface: the natural philosophy of the **Macrocosm and Microcosm** <note>The Renaissance concept that the human being is a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note> born from the spirit of the Renaissance, the solemn feeling of unity and universality of God, the world, and the soul, the high sense of self-awareness, and the intensified interest in...

...humans, the new individual life and the pious, delightful joy in the “Light of Nature,” the critical processing of experiences and, most excellently, his experimental and systematically comparative natural research based on experience. No less does he express himself here particularly regarding his doctrine on the origin of diseases [the doctrine of the five Entities <note>original: "Entia"; Paracelsus taught that diseases spring from five possible "spheres" or influences: the stars, poisons, natural constitution, spirits, or God.</note>] and regarding his famous theory of the three principles: Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt [that is, the three substance-forming qualities].

Further detailed discussions follow concerning his astronomy—which combats astrology <note>Paracelsus distinguished between "astronomy" (the true influence of the heavens) and "astrology" (the superstitious practice of his day).</note>—with its modern thoughts on meteorology and the study of climate, then chemical and pharmaceutical questions, through which we gain a particular insight into Hohenheim's rich medicinal treasury.

The cause, course, and cure of disease are precisely investigated, with special consideration given to stone formations [Tartar <note>original: "Tartarus." Paracelsus used this term to describe stony deposits or calcifications in the body, comparing them to the crust formed in wine barrels.</note>] within the human body. In general, Hohenheim establishes the concepts of healing natural forces here, claiming them especially for his surgery <note>original: "Wundarznei," literally wound-medicine or the practice of treating external injuries.</note>. Detailed thought is given to magnetic and suggestive healing, as well as to “Imagination” [healing through the power of the mind] and women's diseases; however, he strives for the most part with sharp criticism—though sometimes contradicting himself—to expose every superstition.

Contemporary theological questions concerning the veneration of saints and the nature of sects are also discussed abundantly, especially toward the end of the *Work Beyond Wonder* <note>original: "Opus Paramirum"</note>. His actual Christian-humanist “theology,” as it confronts us with such power and clarity in the material that remains in manuscript form today, can be clearly read between the lines in places. Yet here, these thoughts are always placed in the service of natural science and the healing arts; for he who devised them lived—as he says of himself—"in the Divine and in Nature as a mighty master of the earthly light." It comprises five books: In the **First**, the origin of all diseases is treated, which is caused by the effect and influence of the stars. In the **Second**, how all diseases may be born from the poison or impurity that is in food and drink [otherwise called <term>Tartar</term> <note>original: "Tartarus." In the **Fourth**, it is discussed how all kinds of diseases may be inflicted through the spirits of man [namely those which the evil will and desire of man gives birth to from within himself]; these are for the most part "magical" diseases. In the **Fifth**, how man often becomes subject to all diseases through the special, hidden counsel of God.

II. Another <term>Work Beyond Wonder</term> <note>original: "Opus Paramirum."</note>, in whose first and second books or parts the origin and descent of all diseases is treated, as they are naturally born from the breaking down of the <term>Mercury</term>, <term>Salt</term>, and <term>Sulphur</term> of the <term>microcosm</term> <note>original: "Mercurii, Salis und Sulphuris Microcosmici." These were not the common chemicals, but Paracelsus’s "Three Principles" that made up all matter, including the human body or "microcosm."</note>. <sig>I</sig>

# THE TEXT OF THE PARAMIRUM BY THEOPHRASTUS H. <note>Theophraustus von Hohenheim, commonly known as Paracelsus.</note> FOR MEDICAL DILIGENCE

## *FIRST BOOK OF PROLOGUES*

### Number I

### FIRST PROLOGUE

<insert>Y</insert>ou should know that all diseases are healed in five ways: and we thus begin our medicine with the cure, and not with the causes, for the reason that the cure reveals the cause to us. [A]

[A] Our argument is based on this: that there are five ways of healing. This is as much as to say that there are five kinds of medicine, or five arts, or five faculties <term>faculties (faculteten): distinct branches of medical knowledge or specialized "powers" of healing</term>, or five types of physician. Among these five, each one is a sufficient faculty of medicine to heal all diseases. For in five ways, as has been indicated, five faculties of medicine are discovered, where each one for itself should hold the degree <note>original: gradum</note> of a physician—a sufficient physician and a skillful physician—to heal every occurrence of disease and infirmity. This applies to both medicines <note>likely referring to the traditional division of internal physic and external surgery</note>, as he who belongs to one of these same degrees—one of the five faculties—is alone a sufficient physician. And in whichever faculty one wishes to learn, experience, explore, and have the degree proven, as one who wishes to make use of it;

<summary>Paracelsus introduces his revolutionary theory that there are five distinct "faculties" or ways of healing, each capable of curing all diseases. He argues that medical understanding should start with the success of the cure itself, which in turn reveals the true cause of the ailment.</summary>

<keywords>five ways of healing, medical faculties, Paracelsus, theory of medicine, physician degrees, cause and cure</keywords>

--- Page 22 ---
<meta>This page continues the "First Prologue" of Paracelsus's *Paramirum*, concluding the discussion on the necessity of a physician being grounded in one of the five healing faculties. It then transitions into the "Second Prologue," which begins to define the practical divisions of medicine, specifically the relationship between internal medicine and surgery.</meta>

(above that, he should look to his soul, and the sick body,) he should be diligent, so that he is a well-grounded man in his **faculty** <term>faculty (facultet): one of the five specific medical methods or branches of knowledge Paracelsus identifies</term>: experiencing more from within himself than from the patient: and placing the foundation within those [faculties], and not [in] the **subject** <term>subject (subiectum): here meaning the patient’s body as it presents to the doctor</term>, which lies blind before him: and not falling from one into another, wavering like those who are ungrounded in themselves, and making themselves doubtful.

For every **faculty** <note>original: facultas</note> is in itself a sufficient **Theory, Practice** and **Physics** <term>Physics (Physic): in the 16th-century sense, the study of natural philosophy and the workings of the physical world</term>, sufficient for the causes; likewise for the healing of the same. With this, we wish to have concluded the entrance of our first medical <note>original: Arzney</note> description and opening.

### Number II

### SECOND PROLOGUE

**AS** the aforementioned words indicate five types of **faculties** of medicine, and that each **faculty** is and may be without the other, and each is a sufficient physician in both medicines <note>referring to the two traditional branches: internal medicine and surgery</note> for all diseases: So note, that we do not speak in such a manner <note>original: derförmig</note> of five types of healing for five types of causes of all diseases: Rather, we describe five types of healing, where each one of them serves all causes of diseases, as follows hereafter.

Initially, if you wish to be a physician, remember that there are two kinds of you: the **physician of the body** <note>original: Leibartzney, referring to internal medicine</note>, and the **surgeon** <note>original: Wund, literally "wound-doctor" or surgery</note>. Not for the reason of two origins: but for the reason of the two-fold division that every cause has within itself.

For **fever** <note>original: febris</note> and **plague** <note>original: Pestilenz</note> have one origin, but it breaks apart: One part goes into the decay of the internal parts, as **fevers** <note>original: febres</note>, and belongs to the physician of the body: the other part goes into the **plague**, that is, into the center toward the exit <note>referring to how the plague manifests externally, such as through buboes or sores</note>.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that a physician must be deeply grounded in a specific "faculty" of healing rather than wavering between methods. He introduces the distinction between internal medicine and surgery, explaining that while they treat different symptoms—like internal fevers versus external plague sores—they often share a single root cause.</summary>

<keywords>medical faculties, physician's education, internal medicine, surgery, fever, plague, Paracelsian theory, clinical practice</keywords>

--- Page 23 ---
<meta>This page concludes the "Second Prologue" and begins the "Third Prologue" of Paracelsus's *Paramirum*. It follows the previous discussion on the five medical faculties by defining the professional division between internal medicine and surgery based on the direction and visibility of a disease.</meta>

⁋ Through such an explanation, understand a foundation for recognizing both **estates** <term>estates (Stendt): the professional classes or branches of medical practice</term> of physicians. Every disease that goes from the center into the distance <note>that is, spreading from the internal organs outward to the extremities</note> belongs to the **physician** <note>original: Physico</note>: But that which goes from the distance into the center <note>that is, moving from the surface of the body inward</note> is reserved for the **surgeon** <note>original: Chirurgico</note>. ⁋

⁋ Note likewise: whatever moves toward the **emunctories** <term>emunctories (Emunctorien): the organs of the body that naturally filter and carry away waste, such as the lymph nodes or nostrils</term> according to ordained nature, that is entirely a matter of **physics** <note>here meaning internal medicine or natural philosophy</note>: but whatever seeks the unnatural **emunctories** <note>referring to artificial openings like incisions or ulcers</note>, that is a matter of **surgery**. Also, whatever are visible sites of diseases, that is a wound: what is invisible, that is of the body. Thus the **estates** <gloss>internal physicians and surgeons</gloss> of physicians are divided. But how the **sects** <term>sects (Secten): the five specific schools or methods of healing Paracelsus is introducing</term> of physicians behave requires more attention. Although they are divided into estates, there are five sects, and they heal in five ways: there are also five origins of the causes of all diseases, but only one sect for each <note>Paracelsus means that while there are five causes, a doctor of a single "sect" should be able to treat them all using their specific method</note>: that is, every sect, or whatever sect a person belongs to, must know the five origins. But, according to the healing, there are five sects; according to the understanding, based on the knowledge of the causes, there is only one sect. With this, we wish to have concluded the discussion on the estates of physicians. ⁋

## Number III

### THIRD PROLOGUE

**WIE** <note>Initial 'W' is decorated in the original</note> **AS** five types of physicians are found, and also should be, as in the faculties, namely the five sects: and thus they are divided from one another, so that no sect **proceeds** <gloss>acts or operates</gloss> like another; and every sect is sufficient to heal the five origins of all diseases, which every sect must know for itself under its own cure: So first note the names of the five sects, after which we will further investigate medicine once this **preamble** <note>original: praeambulum; an introductory statement</note> is finished. ⁋

<summary>Paracelsus distinguishes between internal physicians and surgeons based on whether a disease moves outward from the body's center or inward from the surface. He then introduces the concept of five medical "sects" or schools of healing that will be the focus of the next section.</summary>
<keywords>estates of medicine, physician, surgeon, emunctories, five sects, origins of disease, internal vs external medicine</keywords>

--- Page 24 ---
<meta>This page continues the "Third Prologue" where Paracelsus begins to define the five distinct sects of medical practice. Following the division between the estates of internal medicine and surgery on the previous page, he now categorizes doctors based on their underlying philosophy and method of treatment.</meta>

The first **faculty** or **sect** is called the **Naturalists**: for the reason that they treat with medicine according to nature alone, just as the concordances <note>original: concordantzen; these were scholastic textbooks that gathered and harmonized the opinions of famous ancient doctors into single summaries</note> agree: such as cold with heat, moist with dry, fullness with emptying, fasting with filling, and the like, just as nature teaches us to drive out each thing through its opposite. Of this sect were **Avicenna**, **Galen**, **Rhazes**, and their commentators, and the like.

The second **sect** is called the **Specifics**: for the reason that they heal all diseases through a **specific form** <note>original: formam specificam</note> and through a **specific essence** <note>original: Ens specificum; the "inner core" or vital power of a substance</note>. For example: a magnet draws iron to itself, which it does not do by the nature of its [elemental] qualities, but by its **specific [power]** <note>original: specifica</note> alone. In this way, these physicians heal all diseases in the **specific cure**. Of these were the **experimenters** and those you call **empirics** <term>empirics: doctors who relied on practical experience and observation rather than the theoretical "humoral" systems of the university-trained Naturalists</term> because of your mockery: and also all **Naturalists** for the reason that they **purge** <term>purge (purgiren): to clear the body of waste or humors, often via laxatives or vomiting</term>, which comes from the **specific form** and does not belong to the **Naturalists**; thus they fall from one **sect** into the other.

The third are called **Characterists**: for the reason that, through their **characters** <term>character (Character): symbolic signs, inscriptions, or spoken words believed to hold magical or healing power</term>, they make all diseases healthy, as their **treatise** <note>original: Libell</note> and their **cure** demonstrate. This occurs with such power as when one commands someone to run, and he runs; that happens through the word: so also is this [healing] through the word, which is a **character**. And their founders and practitioners were **Albertus Magnus**, the **astrologers**, **philosophers**, and many more of them.

The fourth are called the **Spiritualists**: for the reason that they can command and compel the spirits of herbs and roots to release the sick person whom they have captured and afflicted. Just as when a judge puts someone in the **stocks** <note>original: Stock; a wooden restraint for prisoners, also used as a general term for a jail</note>, then he alone is that person's physician:

<summary>Paracelsus defines the first four of his five medical sects: the Naturalists (who treat by opposites), the Specifics (who use the inherent powers of substances), the Characterists (who heal via symbols and words), and the Spiritualists (who command the spiritual forces within nature).</summary>
<keywords>Medical Sects, Naturalists, Galen, Avicenna, Specific Form, Empirics, Characterists, Spiritualists, Albertus Magnus, Renaissance medicine</keywords>

--- Page 25 ---
<meta>This page concludes the description of the five medical sects and introduces the organizational structure of the subsequent books. For the rod is his and the key is his; he may open. Thus, at the same time, he knows how those bound by sickness are released through the **spirit of herbs**, just as that same spirit decays or is consumed; as his **booklet** <note>original: Libell; referring to a small treatise or specific medical manual</note> indicates hereafter. There are many of these sects, too many to name, such as **Hippocrates** and others. The fifth [sect] is called the **Fideles** <note>Latin: "The Faithful"</note>: for the reason that they make diseases healthy through **Faith**, as one who believes in the truth becomes healthy: just as Christ and his disciples did. Regarding such sects, five **definitive books** <note>original: Beschluß Bücher; concluding or authoritative volumes that summarize the findings</note> will follow hereafter, in which we wish to instruct you so that you may understand them **better**.

### Number IV
## FOURTH PROLOGUE

As we indicate to you, in order to arrange five definitive books according to the five sects, we divide them into two parts: one for the **Practice of the Body** <note>Internal medicine</note> and the other for the **Practice of Wounds** <note>Surgery</note>; these are recorded with their **Canons** <term>canons: fundamental rules or authoritative instructional textbooks that hold dogmatic importance</term> and **Paragraphs**. 

But this **preamble** <note>original: praeambel; a preface or introduction</note> and **preface** <note>original: praefagia; used here as a foreword or introductory note</note> we apply significantly to both parts, so that no estate <note>the "estates" of the physician and the surgeon</note> shall be excluded. But before we begin the five books for you, we wish to show you physicians in both estates and in all sects a **Parenthesis**, which shall be set apart as if by a bracket, which we call the **Medical Parenthesis** <note>original: Parenthesin Medicam; a conceptual "bridge" or explanatory chapter inserted between the introduction and the main text</note>. 

This shall stand between the current ongoing prefaces and the five definitive books. It will not be attached to any specific book, nor assigned to any one part, but shall stand entirely on its own. This **Parenthesis** will show you the **origin of all diseases** and from whence they come, which every sect of physicians should know and understand. Once he knows this, the physician has his free will within himself <note>meaning the doctor can then choose the most appropriate method of treatment from the five sects</note>.

<summary>Paracelsus describes the fifth sect of medicine—the "Fideles" who heal through faith—and introduces a "Medical Parenthesis," a standalone section intended to explain the origin of all diseases to both physicians and surgeons.</summary>
<keywords>Fideles, Faith Healing, Medical Parenthesis, Hippocrates, Internal Medicine, Surgery, Origin of Disease, Five Sects</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the organizational layout of the medical treatise. It concludes the explanation of how the five medical sects are integrated into the "Parenthesis" (the explanatory bridge of the work) before starting the "Second Book of Prologues," which addresses the professional conduct and education of physicians and surgeons.</meta>

...to take from among the five **sects** <note>Schools of medical thought described previously</note> whichever he wishes, and to apply them upon the **foundation** of how he understands the origin of diseases, according to the explanation of this **Parenthesis** <note>original: Parenthesis; here used as a title for an explanatory section or bridge that connects the introduction to the main body of the work</note>. This Parenthesis is intended to show you the causes of all diseases: therefore it rightly precedes the five **definitive books** <term>definitive books: original "Beschluß-bücher," the authoritative volumes that summarize the final conclusions of the study</term>, for the reason that healing must have a foundation—that is, a man who is knowledgeable about the basis upon which healing is applied. 

In this Parenthesis, there will be five divisions, called **Tractates**: and there are five of them because there are five things from which all diseases arise. Each Tractate is further divided into chapters, so that the foundation of the origins may be more easily understood, including all accidents, diseases, and their entire lineage, and from whence they come. This will all be presented in double chapters, according to the understanding of both **estates of medicine** <note>Referring to the "Physicians" (internal medicine) and "Surgeons" (external/wound medicine)</note>, following one another in all sects and separated from each other by **Rules** <note>original: Regulas; systematic guidelines for practice</note>. The end of the five tractates marks the end of the Parenthesis, its chapters, and its rules: and then the five definitive books on the foundation of healing within the five sects begin.

❦ Furthermore, we are motivated by the few signs of success you show and the many sick people who resist all of you, and to whom you deny help. Galen was more of a "Characteristic" physician <note>A physician who works with the "characters" or inner signatures and signs of things</note> than a Natural one, and likewise with others. Such faculties and secrets may be called the <term>Great Mysteries of the Art</term> <note>original: "Magnalia Artis"</note>, yet they are suppressed; brought forth by the long way that you chew and ruminate upon. ❦

### THIRD PROLOGUE

**A**s five Beings <note>original: "Entia"</note> have thus been described to you, observe, you physician, what sort of Being is recognized. ## FOURTH PROLOGUE

**A**S we indicate regarding the five **Entities** <term>Entia; from the Latin "ens" (being), these are the five fundamental sources of all disease in Paracelsian medicine</term>, the next task is to recognize these **Entities**. And even if our ancient forefathers, were they to be born again, would find themselves astonished and alienated by our medicines <note>original: "Artzneyen"</note>, that should be the least of our concerns. We do not wish to be horrified by their recipes, but rather to pick out the core essence from within them. At the beginning of this section <note>original: "parenthesis"; used here to mean an introductory discourse or explanatory passage</note>, with which we end the little book of prologues, we aim for you to understand the **Entities**. These are the forces that compel and violently force our body, and it happens thus:

The first treatise of this section explains how the stars <note>original: "Gestirn"</note> have a power and essence within them; this power has mastery over our body, so that our body must wait and receive what the stars work within us. This power of the stars is called the **Being of the Stars** <term>Ens Astrorum; the celestial and astrological influences on human health</term>, and it is the first **Entity** to which we are subject.

The second power that rules over us with authority and brings us into sickness is the **Being of Poison** <term>Ens Veneni; the effect of toxins, diet, or external substances processed by the body</term>. Note here: even if the stars do us no harm and are healthy within us, the **Being of Poison** may yet kill us; we are subject to it and must expect it, for we cannot defend ourselves against it. 

The third is a power that sickens and weakens our body even if the previous two **Entities** within us are good and fortunate; this is called the **Natural Being** <term>Ens Naturale; the body’s own internal biological nature and its inherent tendency to fail or age</term>. This **Entity** is that which makes our own body sick through its own error and through its own internal breakdown. Thus, many other diseases spring from this—indeed all diseases, without exception—even when all other **Entities** are favorable. 

The fourth **Entity** speaks of the powerful spirits <note>original: "Geistern"</note> who sicken and weaken our body; they have authority over it, and we must wait and receive the sicknesses upon our body as they inflict them upon us. The fifth **Entity**,

# TEXT OF THE PARENTHESIS ON THE FIVE BEINGS <note>original: "Textus Parenthesis Superentia Quinq."</note>
## FIRST BOOK OF THE BEINGS OF DISEASES AND THE FIRST PAGAN BEING <note>original: "Liber Entium Morborum Primus et Pagoyum Primum"; "Pagoyum" is Paracelsus's term for natural or "pagan" knowledge as opposed to divine revelation</note>
### TREATISE
#### *ON THE BEING OF THE STARS OVER LOWER BODIES* <note>original: "De Ente Astrorum Super Corpora Inferiora"</note>
#### CHAPTER I

As we are to describe the **Astral Being** <term>Ens Astrale; the star-driven influence or environment that affects human health</term> to you, it is first and most necessary for us to consider the nature, essence, shape, form, and property of the **Stars** <note>original: "Astra"</note>: From this it follows thereafter, in what way the **Astral Being** is drawn out. To that end, you have taken for yourselves a foundation from astronomical teaching, following premature indications; and you do not consider the truth that you ought to consider. Thus, you say that the Heaven makes the body, that is, the **star** <note>original: "astrum"</note>: which is not so. Man is created once **corporally** <note>original: "corporaliter"; in a physical, bodily sense</note>, and nothing further forms him except the **Being of the Seed** <term>Ens Seminis; the internal power or blueprint within the "seed" that determines a person's physical growth</term> alone, without any stars. Based on such [a belief], you indicate that the Stars govern bodies and natures, shape [them], and the like, according to their properties: which is nothing more than a weak <note>original: "lincker"; the contemporary footnote clarifies this as "schwacher" (weak or feeble)</note> dis-

<summary>Paracelsus begins his treatise on the Astral Being (Ens Astrale), the first of the five causes of disease. He challenges traditional astrology, arguing that while stars are influential, they do not create the human body, which is instead formed by the "Being of the Seed."</summary>

...the state is; for it is not so: this will be shown to you in the **Being of the Seed** <term>Ens Seminis; the internal power or blueprint within the "seed" that determines a person's physical growth and inheritance</term>.

Regarding such an opinion of yours, we will **argue** <gloss>original: *arguiren*, from the Latin *arguo*, to prove or demonstrate</gloss> nothing further, for it argues itself through its own **solution** <gloss>original: *solution*, meaning the resolution or explanation of the problem</gloss>.

But on the basis of our parenthesis <note>Paracelsus refers to his explanatory digression as a "parenthesis"</note>, we wish to give you such an enlightenment. Adam and Eve received their bodies through the creation, and through the **Being of the Seed**, until the passing away of the world. And even if no star, no planet had ever existed, and did not exist now, children would still have been born from their birth and given a **complexion** <term>complexion; the physical and temperament-based constitution of a person, not merely skin tone</term> and a nature, just as they are otherwise: one a **Melancholic** <note>original: *Melancholicus*; one of the four humors, traditionally associated with a pensive or somber temperament</note>, the other a **Choleric** <note>original: *Cholericus*; one of the four humors, traditionally associated with an ambitious or quick-tempered nature</note>; one faithful, the other unfaithful; one of a pious nature, the other of an evil nature. Such properties of men are in the **Being of Individuality** <term>Ente proprietatis; the innate individual nature or "peculiarity" of a person</term> <gloss>original: *proprietas* here means peculiarity or character</gloss>, and do not come from the stars: for they [the stars] have no part in the body, that is, they provide no complexion, no color, no form, no property, no nature, no essence.
¶

## CHAPTER II <note>original: "CAPUT II"</note>

**W**E indicate to every physician that he should understand two **Beings** <note>original: "Entia"</note> in man: the **Being of the Seed** and the **Being of Virtue** <term>Ens Virtutis; the internal power, faculty, or vital strength of a human being</term>. Although we indicate nothing further here: nevertheless, be mindful that you read of them in their respective kinds. We speak here of such a foundation that should serve as an introductory text regarding the **Astral Being** <term>Ens Astrale; the influence of the heavens or the environment that affects human health</term>.
¶
Since we wish to instruct you on how the **Astral Being** may harm us: it is a necessity to explain to you that you should first know that the stars—from planets, from stars, and the entire firmament—do nothing to the body, nothing to our color, nothing to our beauty, nothing to our gestures, nothing to our virtues and properties.

...but, they do not become through them. Do not think that the sun makes it, nor the **firmament** <term>the sphere of the stars</term>, or the like: But note this, that the warmth of the sun provides such a period of time. Just as if you want to **digest** <note>original: *digeriren*; in Paracelsian terms, this means to dissolve, soften, or ripen through gentle heat</note> and bring a thing into its full effect, it must happen through a **Digestion** <term>Digest; the process of maturation or ripening, often compared to chemical "digestion" in a lab</term>. This **Digestion** works through nothing other than time: the thing that is inside it has its effect within itself, and understand it thus. **Digestion** <note>original: *Digestio*</note> is such a thing: A child cannot grow without the Digestion, for it grows within the Digestion, that is, in the **womb** <term>Matrice; the uterus or "matrix" where life is formed</term>. And thus the child requires no stars or planets for this: Its mother is its planet and star. The seed must have a Digestion, which is in the soil: but the soil is no Digestion without the sun. The mother, however, is a Digestion without any **stars** <term>Astra</term>. And even if the sun never shone, and **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercurius*</note> went retrograde, children would still thrive and grow; neither their sun nor their Digestion is taken from them. ❦

❦ For the stars have no power at all to incline man toward them, or to compel him to have them. Understand it thus: take two soldiers who are both angry; which one gives his nature to the other? Neither. Two twins who look like each other; which one has it from the other that he looks like him? Neither. Why then do we want to call ourselves **Jovian** <note>original: *Jovische*; children born under the influence of Jupiter</note> children or **Lunar** <note>original: *Monische*; children of the Moon</note> children, since we are like twins toward one another? A child, being like the seed in its essence, is a "twin" <note>In this context, Paracelsus suggests humans share a common internal nature rather than being copies of stars</note> just like the seed, and not a child of the sun, as is written concerning **twins** <note>original: *de Geminis*</note>. ❦

<summary>Paracelsus argues that human growth is an internal process ("Digestion") occurring within the mother's womb, which acts as the child's true "planet," independent of actual celestial movements.</summary>

### CHAPTER IV

**A**fter we have thus indicated this, note further that we wish hereafter to complete the **parenthesis** <term>Parenthesin; here meaning a specific explanatory section or digression</term> regarding the **Astral Entity** <term>Ens Astrale; the influence of the heavens and stars on human health and fate</term>, so that you may understand our premise: how the **stars** <term>Gestirn</term> make us sick and kill us. For you have understood the **stars** <term>Astra</term> until now as if they **incline** <note>original: *incliniren*; referring to the astrological maxim *Astra inclinant, non necessitant* (The stars incline, but do not compel)</note> into us, and that this **inclination** <note>original: *Inclinaß*</note> shapes us according to them. Based on this, you write great **pamphlets** <note>original: *Libell*</note> about how the stars should be resisted—which is just idle talk <note>original: *ein blau schreiben*; literally "writing in blue," an idiom for writing nonsense or falsehoods</note>. We do not concern ourselves with the saying, “A wise man rules over the stars,” as you understand it; but as we understand it, so shall we accept it. They exert no power at all within us, they imprint nothing, they claim nothing, they **incline** nothing: they are free for themselves, and we are free for ourselves.

Now note, however, that we cannot live without the stars: for cold and heat, and the **maturation** <term>Digest; the process of ripening or development through heat</term> of the things that we eat and use, comes from them—except for man himself. And they are useful to us, and we must have them, only as much as we must have cold and heat, food and drink, and air; but they are no further within us, nor are we within them. But if they are equal to us, or we to them—or if you are not like them, or they are [not] like us—why then should we make such great **propositions** <note>original: *propositiones*</note> and **disputes** <note>original: *disputationes*</note>? Thus the **Creator** <term>Fabricator; the Divine Architect or Maker of the world</term> willed it to be. Who knows what is in the firmament that we do not know, which serves that very purpose? 

For the purity of the Sun profits us nothing, nor the art of **Mercury** <note>original: *Mercury*</note>, nor the beauty of **Venus** <note>original: *Veneris*</note>: only the shine from the Sun profits us, in that it creates the fruit and the summer, wherein our nourishment grows. But to conclude this speech, so that the **parenthesis** may be opened for you, note this: A child who is born, or conceived under the best planets and stars, and in the most virtuous ones according to every wish—if it has the opposite in its own nature, and is entirely perverse, whose [fault] is...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that while the stars provide the necessary environment for life (heat and seasons), they do not exert direct astrological control over human character or health. ### CHAPTER V

**B**EFORE we come to our proposition <note>original: *Propositum*</note>, we wish to set before you a matter concerning the aptitude of the body. Since you consider it so much and so well—believing that man receives his fortune and his aptitude from the stars, such that one person grows more than another: one in the arts, another in riches, a third in power, and so forth. You attribute such things to the stars, believing you receive them from their influence; we distance ourselves from this view and explain it in this way:

Fortune comes from aptitude, and aptitude comes from the spirit. According to whatever spirit a person has, so is he suited for a specific thing; and according to his aptitude for that thing, so does he have fortune. So that you may understand this spirit, it is like an **Archeus** <term>Archeus; the internal "master craftsman" or vital force that governs the body's functions</term>: as is written in *On the Archeus* <note>original: *de Archeo*</note>, which we shall not discuss further here, lest we depart from our purpose. First, take note that you have several diseases occurring in the body which affect the **Vital Fluid** <note>original: *Liquorem Vitae*; the essential life-sustaining moisture of the body</note>; these cause bodily diseases. The others are those that cause wounds <note>In this context, "wounds" often refers to external sores, ulcers, or skin eruptions</note>; these are those that affect the **Expulsive Power** <note>original: *Virtutem Expulsivam*; the body’s natural ability to push out or excrete harmful substances</note>. Thus, in these two, all **Theory** <note>original: *Theoric*</note> stands.

### Part I

**A**S we thus show you how the **Astral Influence** <note>original: *Ens Astrale*</note> sickens us with bodily and wound-diseases: specifically, those diseases that do not leave the body, and those diseases that do leave the body. So you should know that we are not recounting to you here how the poison lies in every single star; for that is more a matter of Astronomy than Medicine.

But however it may be, there are five kinds of poison that cause dropsy: and it is of one form, but of five properties. Thus, one is a poison of the stars, and the other four belong to the other **Influences** <note>original: *Ens*; Paracelsus taught that there are five "Entia" or origins of disease: Stars, Poison, Nature, Spirits, and God</note>, yet they all cause dropsy; just as there are five kinds of Sulfur and the like.

<summary>Paracelsus classifies astral poisons according to alchemical categories (mercurial, salty, etc.), explaining how they target specific organs or bodily functions like the "Vital Fluid." He distinguishes between internal diseases and external "wounds," noting that while stars cause illness, their specific astronomical positions are less important to the physician than their chemical effects.</summary>

### Part II

**H**ow you are to recognize these same things—from which **Influence** <term>Ens; literally 'being' or 'essence', referring here to one of the five primary causes of disease in Paracelsian medicine</term> the **dropsy** <note>original: *wassersucht*; a buildup of fluid in the body, known today as edema</note> arises, and with what medicine it should be healed: that same information is found in *On the Treatments of Diseases* <note>original: *de morborum medicationibus*</note>. And so we wish to conclude this section on the **Influence** <note>original: *Ens*</note>; further indicating that you should not think to treat an **Astral disease** <note>original: *Astralische kranckheit*; an illness caused by celestial forces</note> while the specific star that caused it still rules: for the star is more powerful than the physician. In this regard, you should remember to observe the proper time if you wish to be true physicians: and do not attempt to force any disease toward healing before its time, for it simply will not happen.

## TREATISE
### *ON THE ESSENCE OF POISON* <note>original: *DE ENTE VENENI*</note>
#### CHAPTER I

**D**irectly following our description of the **Astral Essence** <term>Ens Astrale; the first of the five causes of disease, relating to celestial and atmospheric influences</term>, we now present to you the **Essence of Poison** <term>Ens Veneni; the second cause of disease, involving toxins or impurities found in the food and drink we consume</term>, which is the second thing that sickens our bodies. And here we establish a foundation similar to the one we held regarding the **Astral Essence** <note>original: *Ente Astrali*</note>: namely, that our body is compelled and forced to suffer because of five **Essences** <term>Entibus; plural of *Ens*, the five fundamental causes of disease in Paracelsian medicine</term>. But so that you may understand and grasp our meaning more easily, we will leave such matters to the **prefaces** <note>original: *Praefatzen*</note> and explain the foundation of the **Essence of Poison** <note>original: *Entis Veneni*</note> to you in this way.

You know that our bodies must have a "containment"—that is, a management or guidance—through which they are sustained and nourished; and where that is not present, in 그 place there is no life. Regarding this, take note: He who created and made our bodies also made our nourishment just like the body—quite good, but not quite perfect. Understand us correctly here: The body is given to us without **poison** <note>original: *gifft*</note>, and within it there is no poison. However, in that which we must give to the body for its nourishment, there is poison.

## CHAPTER II <note>original: CAPUT II</note>

But to the grass itself, it is no poison. Man, whatever he eats and drinks, that same thing is both poison and health to him. ### CHAPTER IV <note>original: CAPUT IV</note>

**D**rom this you should fathom the Creator: since all things are perfect in themselves, and ordained by the Creator so that one must contain the other—the grass the cow, the cow the human. The peacock eats snakes, **lizards** <note>original: Lacerten; from Latin lacerta</note>, and the **spotted lizard** <note>original: Stellionem; referring to the Stellio, a lizard with star-like spots, often mentioned in early natural histories</note>. Thus, consider that every animal has its own nourishment, which is assigned to it as food, and for that purpose an Alchemist is ordained for it to separate it. To the **ostrich** <note>original: Straussen; it was a common early modern belief that ostriches could digest iron</note>, the Alchemist is given to separate iron—that is, the **waste** <note>original: Stercus; Latin for dung or excrement</note> from the **nutrient** <note>original: Nutriment</note>—which is possible for no other [creature].

## CHAPTER V

**J**ust as we have shown you concerning the Alchemist, consider now that the Alchemist is appointed by the Creator alone for this reason: that he separates the good from that which does not belong to the "good," for the benefit of the one who consumes it as nourishment for his body, just as the Creator fashioned it. So, mark from this point forward our beginning: that there are five things that have power over man, and man is subject to them. These are the <term>Astral Entity</term> <note>original: Ens Astrale; the influence of the stars and atmosphere on the body</note>, which we have already described to you, and following that, the <term>Entity of Poison</term> <note>original: Ens Veneni; the influence of toxins found in food and drink</note>. ❦

❦ Now, if a person is healthy and untroubled by all the stars, he still has no guarantee against the **Entity of Poison**, but must wait to see how it might overpower him. We shall leave that as it stands, just as we left it in the **prefaces** <note>original: proemiis</note>. ❦

❦ However, so that you may recognize this well and easily, mark the first principle, which will show you how poison may and does harm you: Since we have an **Alchemist** <note>Note the manner in which—here as in the preceding text—purely scientific-medical metaphors are introduced.</note> within us, who [separates] us from the—

# CHAPTER VI

**T**hus you should understand that the **Astronomers** <note>In the 16th century, "astronomy" and "astrology" were often used interchangeably to describe the study of celestial influences on Earthly bodies</note> err once again when they point out our bodily failings and posit a fortunate and healthy body. If this health does not occur, it is caused solely by the fact that the other **Entities** <note>original: Entia; the five fundamental causes of disease in Paracelsian medicine</note>, of which there are four more, weaken the body, and not the **Stars** <note>original: Astra</note>. Therefore, we may well laugh at their writings and snicker when they so certainly promise health, for they do not consider that there are still four other **Entities** which are just as powerful as the **Star** <note>original: Astrum</note>. But we must joke with them: What is a cat without a mouse, or a prince without a fool? The **Physiognomist** <note>original: Physiomanticus; one who predicts health or character based on physical appearance</note> also carries on with such a tale that does not make us weep: he promises health and does not think that there are four **Entities** that he does not understand. For he speaks out of the **Natural Entity** <note>original: Ente naturali; the internal nature or constitution of the individual</note> and remains silent about the others, which amuses us just a tiny bit. It requires a well-knowing man to predict [the things] that happen from the courses. For the courses are five, and there is only one man: whichever courses he forgets while proceeding with the others, he may well be a "blue prophet" <note>an idiomatic term for a false or unreliable prophet</note>. To divide these influences, and to speak according to that division—each according to what he has learned, what they indicate and toward what—that is what we greatly praise, and we praise such a man. For instance, when the **Pyromantic Specialist** <note>original: Entist pyromanticus; one who studies the Entity of Spirits or fire</note> places a **Judgment** <note>original: Judicium; a formal medical or astrological verdict</note> upon the spirits; and the **Physiognomic Specialist** <note>original: Entist physionomus</note>, who places it upon the nature of the man himself; and the **Theological Specialist** <note>original: Entist Theologicus</note> upon the course of God...

## CHAPTER VII

**T**O give you a foundation concerning the Alchemist, understand this: God has given every creature its own being and that which belongs to it. This is not for the sake of its own self-governance or the like, but for the sake of use—that which is necessary for it and which it must have—which is accompanied by poison. Within the body, there is one who separates this poison from that which the body absorbs. This is the Alchemist <note>In Paracelsian medicine, the "Alchemist" (also called the Archeus) is an internal spirit or force that acts as a celestial pharmacist, separating nutrients from waste</note>, for the reason that he employs the Art of Alchemy. He separates the evil from the good; he transforms the good into a **Tincture** <note>original: Tinctur; a vital, health-giving essence extracted from food</note>; he tinctures the body for its life; he prepares the matter within nature; he tinctures it so that it becomes blood and flesh. This Alchemist lives in the stomach <note>original: Magen</note>, which is his instrument, wherein he cooks and works. And understand it in this way: When a person eats meat, there is both poison and goodness within it. But in his eating, he perceives it all as good, for the poison lies hidden beneath the good, and beneath the evil there is no good. Thus, as soon as the food—that is, the meat—enters the stomach, the Alchemist is immediately there and performs the separation. That which does not contribute to the health of the body, he casts into a special place; the good he sends to its proper place where it belongs. This is an ordinance of the Creator <note>original: Schöpffer</note>. In this way, the body is sustained so that no harm from the poison it eats befalls it; instead, it is separated by the Alchemist without the person's own effort. Such is the virtue and power of the Alchemist within man. ❦

### CHAPTER VIII

**N**OW observe further, that in every thing a human takes for their necessity, there is a poison hidden beneath the good. Thus: in every thing there is an **Essence** <note>original: Essentia; the life-sustaining part of a substance</note> and a **Poison** <note>original: Venenum</note>. **Essence** is that which sustains the human: <gloss>1) sustains</gloss>. **Poison** <gloss>2) poison</gloss> is that which inflicts sickness upon them. This is found in every thing used for nourishment, even for animals; nothing is exempt. Take note of this, you physicians: Since the body relies on nourishment and must have it, and is subject to it, it must take it as it finds it, in both forms, good and evil, with nothing yet separated. It must leave it to the **Alchemist** <note>In Paracelsian thought, the "Alchemist" or "Archeus" is the internal spirit that governs digestion and separates nutrients from toxins</note> to separate those very things.

So note: if the **Alchemist** is faulty <gloss>3) frail or defective</gloss>, so that the poison cannot be separated from the good according to the perfect manner of the art, then the poison and the good become a unified **decay** <gloss>4) decay or putrefaction</gloss> <note>original: putrefactio</note>, and thereafter a **Digestion** <note>original: Digestio</note>. This is what reveals the diseases of humanity. For every disease a person has—aside from the **Entity of Poison** <note>original: Ens Veneni; one of Paracelsus's five categories of disease causes, specifically those originating from external toxins</note>—comes to them from a decayed **Digestion**. This digestion should remain in a balanced state so that the **Alchemist** finds no point of imbalance. But if the **Digestion** is broken, the **Alchemist** is not perfect in his **instrument**. Then **corruption** <note>original: corruptio</note> <gloss>5) rot or corruption</gloss> follows. 

This corruption is the mother of all diseases, which should be thoroughly understood by you physicians, rather than your usual long-winded explanations. For **corruption** poisons the body according to its nature and what it becomes. For example: a water that is pure and clear may be tinted <note>original: tingirt; a term from alchemy meaning to change the color or quality of a substance</note> to whatever color one wishes. Likewise, the body is like water, and the **corruption** is the color; and there is no color that does not have its origin in poison, and it is a sign and token of its poison.

<summary>Paracelsus explains that every substance contains both life-sustaining essence and harmful poison, requiring the "Internal Alchemist" to separate them. Disease arises when this internal process fails, leading to "corruption" that tints the body like a dye in water.</summary>

# CHAPTER IX

**S**O that we may give you a better understanding, understand that **corruption** <note>original: corruptio; the biological breakdown or decay of substances</note> occurs in two ways: **locally** and **through the cleansing organs** <note>original: localiter and emunctorialiter</note>¹) and it happens like this. When it is thus in the **digestion** <note>original: Digest; referring to the digestive process or the stomach itself</note>, and the Alchemist <note>the internal force that separates nutrients from toxins</note> is overcome during the separation due to a defect in the failing digestion: then in that very place a **decay** <note>original: fäule; putrefaction</note> is **generated**, which is a poison. For every decay is a poison to the place in which it lies, and is a mother of a certain deadly poison. For the decay spoils the good, and when that good is removed from its proper function, then the poison overcomes the good; it is seen in no other way than in the form of the good substance which lies there in decay: thus it becomes a mother of the diseases that are subject to it. 

But as for that which is **through the cleansing organs**, that occurs through the error of Nature in the expulsion, in this way: When the Alchemist expels the poison—each poison through its own **cleansing organ** <note>original: emunctorium; a biological waste-disposal channel</note>: white **sulfur** <note>original: sulphur; in this context, a metabolic byproduct representing the "combustible" principle</note> through the nose; **arsenic** <note>original: arsenic; here referring to a specific volatile waste product, not just the chemical element</note> through the ears; and likewise **excrement** <note>original: stercus</note> through the **rectum** <note>original: monoculum; literally "the one-eye," a term used for the lower bowel or anus</note>; and so other poisons, each according to how it is assigned to its cleansing organ. If one of these same poisons is hindered, whether through the weakness of Nature, by its own accord, or similar causes: then that too is a mother of the diseases subject to it. Thus there are two origins **universally** <note>original: universaliter</note> in all diseases, which we will not show you further here: But you will find them in the *Books on the Origin of Diseases in Particular* <note>original: Libris de Origine Morborum in speciali</note>.

# CHAPTER X

**A**S has been indicated above regarding the Alchemy of Nature, how it resides in every animal and exists for the necessity of the separation which must take place in the stomach: so mark a brief—

# INTERPOSED PARENTHESES
## THE THIRD BOOK AND THE THIRD PAGOYUM <note>A term coined by Paracelsus, likely referring to a specific division or "region" of his philosophical system</note>
### TREATISE
### *ON THE NATURAL ENTITY* <note>original Latin: "DE ENTE NATURALI"</note>
### CHAPTER I

**A**ccordingly, you physicians may well perceive a strange contradiction within yourselves between the <term>Natural Entity</term> <note>The "Ens Naturale" refers to the biological and astrological nature of the individual, specifically the "inner firmament" or the biological clock and constitution unique to each person</note> and your own medical writings. However, let us not burden ourselves with that here; instead, we shall point out the **Natural Entity**, which is the third entity following our <term>Parentheses</term> <note>Paracelsus views the various "Entities" or causes of disease as distinct sections or "parentheses" in the study of medicine</note>. From this entity, every kind of **disease** can and will be born whenever the **Natural Entity** undergoes such a change as the following chapters will describe to you.

To begin, mark well what the **Natural Entity** is: and if, in our explanation of it, we do not use your mother tongue or the language you learned while you sat in school during your first lessons or in **Heinrichmann** <note>Jacob Heinrichmann (c. 1482–1561) was a humanist grammarian. Paracelsus is mocking traditional academic education which prioritized Latin grammar over the actual study of nature</note>: then consider the new power [of this teaching] and the foolishness of those old, wasted men.

The **Natural Entity** is this: You are aware of **Influence** <note>the "in-flowing" of power from the heavens to the earth</note> in **astronomy**, the **firmament**, and all the stars; and you know the stars,

However, as for how we define digestion, we shall leave that to the <term>Alchemist</term> <note>In Paracelsian terms, the "Internal Alchemist" or "Archaeus" is the force that separates the useful from the waste</note>—that is, the peasant who produces manure on the field. - The brain is the **Moon**
- The heart is the **Sun**
- The spleen is **Saturn**
- The lungs are **Mercury**
- The kidneys <gloss>original: "Renes"</gloss> are **Venus**

In the same manner that the upper firmaments conduct their course and bring forth their effects, so you must understand it here. For if you wish to know the **crisis** <gloss>original: "Crisim"; the turning point or progression of a disease</gloss>, you must recognize the natural course within the body. If you do not recognize this, you cannot determine the "crisis" of **natural diseases** <note>original: "morbos naturales"</note> arising from the **Natural Entity** <note>original: "Ente naturali"; the biological/astrological influence on health, one of Paracelsus's five "Entia" or causes of disease</note>. For you will find that your clinical "crisis" and the celestial "crisis" are two very different things, as you shall clearly see.

# CHAPTER V

**S**O, we wish to give you instruction on how to find the **crisis** <note>original: "Crisim"; in a medical context, the "crisis" is the turning point of a disease where the patient either recovers or declines</note>, as far as belongs to this **parenthesis** <note>original: "Parenthesi"; here meaning a digression or specific section of the argument</note>, and it is like this. When a child is born, its internal firmament is born with it, along with the seven organs which have the power within themselves to be the seven planets. And thus, the child contains the whole firmament as it pertains to a firmament. For when we speak of the firmament, we mean a complete and perfect firmament, not an empty one; and this is perfectly present within the child.

This internal firmament of the child takes on its **predestination** <note>original: "Praedestinationem"; the pre-determined path or lifespan of a being</note> at its birth. It works like this: when the **creation** <note>original: "Creatz"; the physical formation and birth</note> is perfectly established in the child, at that very same moment the **predestination** <note>original: "Praedestinatz"</note> is also established. This predestination determines how long the **natural entity** <note>original: "Ens Naturale"; the biological force or essence of life</note> shall run. Suppose the creation happens at a specific hour; the end of this creation is set right alongside it—for example, in the 30th year. For the creation and its essence are capable of this, because nature knows—and possesses it within her—how long the natural entity should proceed, and for how many years. 

Take this example: an hourglass that you set and let run. As soon as it starts running, you know exactly at which point it will be empty. Likewise, nature is within the **created being** <note>original: "Creato"</note> such that it knows how long the natural entity will run, and thus how long it runs and ought to run. Therefore, according to that designated time, the **entity of nature** <note>original: "Ens Naturae"</note> and the creation set all the courses belonging to the physical planets within the body, so that they are all completed in the time between the creation and the predestination. 

Take another example. A child is born at a certain hour and is meant to live ten hours according to its natural entity, because its predestination in the **created entity** <note>original: "Ente Creato"</note> was arranged in that way. In that case, the physical organs <gloss>the internal planets</gloss> are all fulfilled in their course <note>original: "lauff"; meaning the organs perform their full biological cycle or "destiny," even if compressed into a short time. As the original note suggests: the child has all the same organs and functions as a hundred-year-old man, but their activity is compressed into a shorter duration so it is used up quickly.</note> just as if—

## CHAPTER VI

**T**HEREFORE, we give you to understand that the heavenly firmament was born once and lasts as long as mankind: for this reason, it has born its course and its predestination once, and produces nothing young. ### Section I

# TEXT OF THE PARENTHESIS REGARDING THE FIFTH ENTITY
<note>original: "TEXTUS PARENTHESIS SUPER ENS QUINTUM". A parenthesis in this context is an explanatory interlude or bridge between major sections of the work.</note>

## THE FIFTH BOOK AND NOT PAGOYUS
<note>original: "LIBER QUINTUS ET NON PAGOYUS". The term "Pagoyus" is a Paracelsian term likely derived from "pagan" or "heathen," referring to those who operate outside of Christian revelation.</note>

### TREATISE
### *ON THE ENTITY OF GOD*
<note>original: "DE ENTE DEI". This refers to diseases or conditions originating directly from God's will or providence, rather than natural or spiritual causes.</note>

#### CHAPTER I

**AS WE** have previously indicated to you at the beginning of our books, we intended to describe some four books according to pagan custom, for the reason that any Christian who writes otherwise than what the faith holds within him, that same man writes as a pagan. Therefore, we wish to depart from those same pagan customs in our Parenthesis, and we will henceforth speak in a Christian style <note>original: "Stylo"</note>, and describe the fifth book, the *Entity of God* <note>original: "Entis Dei"</note>, so that you may no longer accuse us of being pagan. 

Although it is the case that after concluding this Parenthesis we shall begin five books on Practice <note>original: "Practic"; referring to the practical application of these theories in medicine</note>, so that this book may be completed: you should know, however, that in the fifth book we still intend to conclude in a Christian style, and contain the four others—as indicated to you in the beginning—according to pagan custom. We may do this without harm to our faith, for the reason that pagan custom... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page</note>

### CHAPTER V

### Part I <note>original: "Particula I"</note>

**J**ust as we show you the <term>Entity of God</term> <note>original: "Ens Dei"</note>, you should finally resolve that you shall in no way rely on your own certainty in your arts—no matter how experienced you are—for that is to act like a pagan. Instead, you should always direct yourselves toward the Entity of God; that is Christian, and it will go well for you. # PROLOGUE TO THE FIVE BOOKS
## OF THE PRACTICE OF THE PARAMIRUM BY THEOPHRASTUS HOHENHEIM BEGINS

->To the fair and impartial reader, greetings.<-

Favorable, dear reader, since Theophrastus Paracelsus—in the small books of prologues to this *Paramirum*, as well as specifically in the immediately preceding conclusion—actually and expressly reports that he intends to describe five books on **Practice** <note>original: "Practick"; referring to the clinical application of his medical theories</note> belonging to this *Paramirum*, which should follow after the **Parenthesis**. You might perhaps harbor a suspicion that these books were withheld from the public good out of ill-will, because they are lacking here and do not follow the **Medical Parenthesis** (as he calls it) according to the author's promise. Therefore, it was particularly necessary to report in a few words, and to assure you hereby, that those same five **Practical Books** <note>original: "Libri Practici"</note> were not found with these theoretical ones. 

For in the papers <note>original: "Chartis"</note> upon which the author recorded this theory for himself, he wrote no more, but ended with this title: *Prologue to the Five Books of Practice*, and left nearly three sheets of quarto paper blank. This can be seen from the author’s **autograph** <note>original: "Autographo"; the manuscript in the author's own handwriting</note>, which is still in the possession of the highly learned Dr. Johannes Homelius the Younger <note>original: "Secundo"; likely referring to the second of that name in a family of physicians</note>, Doctor of Medicine in Pettau in Styria <note>modern-day Ptuj, Slovenia</note>. 

Whether Paracelsus wrote and completed that same **Practice** in a separate book cannot be known for certain. He was indeed very much in the habit of not binding or stitching together books that belonged together. It could, therefore, well be that they still lie hidden in some other location, currently unknown. However, to my knowledge, I have never heard of anyone who has seen such five **Practical Books**, or knew where they might be preserved. But should God and **Fate** <note>original: "Fatum"</note> grant that they be found in time and come into my hands, they shall not be withheld from the public good.

Therefore, may you be pleased to accept and be satisfied with what can be had at this time. But what is not

¹) <note>The following are the main ideas of Paracelsus's Doctrine of the Three Principles (Tria Prima). Here, the concept of matter appears—in contrast to the standard views of his time—in a more chemical and less symbolic way. Sulfur, Mercury [quicksilver], and Salt are the actual building blocks and forces of materiality; they are the three substance-forming qualities. They correspond to the physical phenomena of combustibility [oiliness], liquefaction [volatility/fluidity], and solidification [firmness]. Sulfur, Mercury, and Salt, which thus also compose the human being, relate in a higher sense to the soul [substance], spirit [attribute], and body [form]. It is a mystical correspondence and unification between the natural and the psychological, between the world and man. Whatever heaven and earth contain and experience is also present within man. Therefore, the same symbolic representations apply to both, as they emerge from a sense of universal unity.</note>

But it is even more sensible: In man, there is nothing that makes him a <term>physician</term> <note>original: "Artzet"</note>. Although he possesses a **distinguished intellect** <note>original: "Praeclarum Ingenium"; here referring to a person's natural talent or noble mental capacity.</note>, there is no art within it. But the <term>physician</term> is not like that; even if he already has the medicine and the patient, he still does not possess the **Science** <note>original: "Scientiam," meaning systematic knowledge or technical mastery.</note> and the <term>understanding</term> of things. Thus, the **excellence of intellect** is a chest for medicine and its **science**; but from the fire comes the treasure that is to be kept within it. Therefore, just as the glassmaker derives his glassmaking from the fire—he who did not know beforehand what he was making, yet retained the art—so too does the fire teach the <term>wisdom</term> and art of medicine; this is the test of the <term>physician</term>.

Thus you comprehend the elements, the **three substances**, the 4 **Stars** <note>original: *Astra*</note>, 4 **Earths** <note>original: *Terras*</note>, the 4 **Waters** <note>original: *Aquas*</note>, the 4 **Fires** <note>original: *Ignes*</note>, the 4 **Airs** <note>original: *Aeres*</note>, and all the 
conditions, morals, properties, and natures of the man, 
without which there is no [sickness]: which you have forgotten 
in that place where you describe the origin of diseases 
as coming from the 4 <term>humors</term> <note>The traditional fluids (blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm) thought to govern health.</note>, which yet have never had 
any fellowship with the elements, nor the four, nor the three. 
It must be spoken of in such a way that every human-like quality 
is found in the sickness, and it be called a "man"; 
who is then born out of the perfect <term>Limbus</term> <note>original: *Limbo*; in Paracelsian philosophy, the "Great Limbus" is the primordial matter or "matrix" from which the entire universe and man were extracted.</note>, just like the sickness.

### CHAPTER THREE

**NECESSITY** is in these things a greater explanation, 
since the sicknesses have been created in such a way, 
and should thus be understood as "man-like." 
Now it is thus: **Sulfur** is a humor, **Mercury** a humor, **Salt** a humor; 
thus there are three of them: these three...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases should be treated as autonomous, individual entities—like a person—rather than abstract imbalances of the traditional four humors. <meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s radical redefinition of disease. Having previously argued that diseases are like "living men" or autonomous entities rather than simple imbalances, he now explains that the traditional "humors" (the four fluids of the body) are merely the physical containers or "bodies" of disease, while the true active cause is a "masculine" or astral spark acting upon substances like Sulfur.</meta>

<term>Humors</term> <note>In ancient medicine, these were the four fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to control health.</note> are, however, **bodies**. A "body" here is a humor, not a foreign thing: the physical frame itself is the very thing that the physician should treat. And although you might wish to say that the humor was the cause that created the sickness, that is not the case: a humor creates no sickness. That which creates the sickness is something else, namely the **Essence of Substance** <note>original: *Substantiae Ens*</note>. Now, everything that creates the sickness must be <term>masculine</term> <note>Paracelsus uses "masculine" to describe the active, initiating, or "seeding" force of a disease, as opposed to the passive "feminine" matter it acts upon.</note>, that is, **astral**, coming from the whole <term>Limbus</term> <note>The primordial "chaos" or matrix from which all physical matter was created.</note>. Since the humor, as it is understood, only possesses what it takes from the **Stars** <note>original: *Astris*</note>, it cannot create the disease itself. Therefore, the sickness should rightly be called "masculine," because of the masculine nature that creates it. Based on this, know what the three are that are here called the cause and the "sickness-makers."

The first is **Sulfur**: Now know its power, that it does not turn toward its own evil by itself, unless it be **astral**—that is, that a spark of fire be thrown into it. Only then does it become masculine, having conceived from the spark. Is not burning masculine, or a masculine effect? Without this effect, nothing happens. Therefore, when a sickness is explained as coming from Sulfur, the Sulfur should first be identified by its specific name: thereafter its masculine effect, and what it was that ignited it. 

There are many kinds of **Sulfurs**: 
<term>Resin</term> <margin>Resin</margin>, 
<term>Gum</term> <margin>Mucilaginous sap from trees</margin>, 
<term>Turpentine</term> <margin>Turpentine</margin>, 
<term>Fat</term> <margin>Fat, lard, or pork fat</margin>, 
<term>Grease</term> <margin>Fatness</margin>, 
<term>Butter</term> <margin>Butter</margin>, 
**Oil**, 
**Burning Wine** <note>original: *Vinum Ardens*; distilled alcohol or spirits</note>, etc. 

Some are sulfurs of wood, some of animals, some of humans, some of metals—such as **Oil of Gold**, **of the Moon** <note>Silver</note>, **of Mars** <note>Iron</note>, etc. Some are of stones, such as **Liquor of Marble**, **of Alabaster**, etc. Some are of seeds, and all other things, designated by their own distinct names. And then the fire within them is accidental—which alone is the **Star** <note>original: *Astrum*; the vital/celestial influence</note>—with its own name: now, this effect is the **Sinning Matter** <note>original: *Materia peccans*; the physical substance that has become the vehicle for disease</note> on its part.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that physical humors are passive "bodies" and not the cause of disease; instead, disease is caused by an active "masculine" or astral spark (fire) igniting different types of "Sulfur" within the body.</summary>
