# Paracelsus, *Paramirum*

Now, regarding **Salt**, it is to be understood that it is in itself a <term>material humor</term> <note>original: *Humor materialis*; Paracelsus uses this to mean a physical, passive substance or fluid in the body.</note>, and it causes no disease unless its **Astral force** <note>original: *Astrum*; the active, celestial power or "blueprint" that gives a physical substance its specific behavior.</note> is present with it. Its Astral force is **Resolution** <note>original: *Resolutio*; the process of dissolving, breaking down, or liquefying a solid into a reactive state.</note>, which makes it <term>masculine</term> <note>For Paracelsus, "masculine" refers to the active, initiating, or "seeding" force of a disease, while "feminine" is the passive matter it acts upon.</note>. For just as a **Spirit of Vitriol** <note>Sulfuric acid.</note>, **Tartar**, **Alum**, **Niter**, etc., manifest themselves with all turbulence when they are dissolved: where would such a nature come to the humors without the Stars? About this, all physicians have remained silent. And if they had made no other error than omitting the Astral force in all causes and cures, that would be proof enough that they have built on moss and sand. Know, therefore, that there are many types of **Salts**: some are **Lime**, others **Ashes** <margin>Ashes.</margin>, others **Arsenical**, others **Antimonial**, others **Marcasitical**, and the like; all of these spring forth and become a specific disease according to what the **Body of Salt** <note>original: *Corpus Salis*</note> is; therefore, each has its own name and property.

Understand also concerning **Mercury**: it is not masculine unless the Astral force of the **Sun** sublimates it; otherwise, it does not rise. There are many preparations of it, but only one **Body**. However, this Body is not like Sulfur or Salt, which have many different bodies—which is why they produce many kinds of Salts and Sulfurs. Here [in Mercury] there is only one Body, but the Astral force prepares it in many ways and in many forms. Therefore, many diseases come from it. Thus, its masculine nature comes from the Astral force, which leads it into diseases. In this way, all diseases are contained within these three [Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury], under their names and titles. Therefore, know now that whatever is **Sulfurous** should be made into **Sulfur**, so that it may burn; and whatever is **Mercury** should be brought into a **sublimation** <note>The process of a substance rising as vapor; Paracelsus uses this to describe the active, volatile state of a disease.</note>, as much as is fit to be sublimated; and whatever is of **Salt** should be brought into a Salt, according to its nature. Thus, the common causes of diseases are understood here, as stated above.

<summary>Paracelsus explains that Salt and Mercury, like Sulfur, only cause disease when activated by "Astral" forces that transform them from passive matter into active, "masculine" agents. He argues that traditional medicine fails because it ignores these celestial influences in favor of mere physical humors.</summary>

Thus it remains as stated above: that man is established in three things, and these three possess a middle <term>body</term> <note>original: *Corpus*</note>, which is the living **body**. For before this life there is <term>prime matter</term> <note>original: *prima materia*; the formless, original state of a substance before it takes a specific shape.</note>, and after this life there is <term>ultimate matter</term> <note>original: *ultima materia*; the final state of a thing after it has completed its purpose or decayed.</note>. This living body is a middle point between the first and the last; it is for the sake of this middle state that the physician and medicine exist. 

Now, although the middle body is the most prominent part, it is not the <term>subject</term> <note>original: *Subiectum*; here, Paracelsus means the actual "material" that the physician works upon.</note> of medicine. Rather, the subject is solely the three **substances** themselves—setting aside the life, essence, kind, and nature, for we have no power to add to or change those things. 

However, that which is our <term>subject</term> [the three substances] breaks down within itself in three ways:

First, it can break through itself. When this happens, it drives itself away from life. For life is like peace: where there is peace, there is unity, and as soon as that unity is unlocked, peace is also unlocked and departs. So it is with life: if the three substances do not wish to remain undivided within the body, life departs, leaving the body dead and broken. 

The second way is when we break it through our own transgressions—whether in birth, in our upbringing, or by our own will—through which we direct and invite the **stars** to rule over us, like a city that brings a harsh master upon its own neck <note>A metaphor for a person whose lifestyle or choices "summon" negative celestial influences or diseases.</note>. 

And thirdly, if the body does not break or separate by its own nature, and if we do not cause it through external means, then comes the third way: the **End**. All things have an end; no matter how good, strong, or beautiful they may be, they all reach an end in time. Thus man is also committed to his end, and to his season and number of years, which is small.

Now we must also consider the reason why there are three things and not just one, and why so many and various <term>species</term> <note>original: *Species*; distinct types or categories of natural things.</note> have been created within them, which are beyond counting. There are so many <term>species</term> that <term>Rhaetian resin</term> <note>original: *Resina Rhetia*; a medicinal resin from the Rhaetian Alps.</note> is not the same as <term>Noric resin</term> <note>original: *Resina Norica*; resin from the Noricum region, roughly modern Austria.</note>, nor is <term>Neapolitan oil of almonds</term> <note>original: *Oleum Amygdalarum Neapolitanum*</note>...

<summary>Paracelsus explains that the human body is a temporary "middle body" sustained by the unity of three substances (Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury). He describes how health is lost through internal discord, human error that invites negative celestial influence, or the natural inevitable end of life.</summary>

### CHAPTER FOUR

**N**ow an error has arisen, which is proposed regarding the <term>complexions</term>¹ <note>original: *Complexionen*; the medieval and Renaissance belief that a person's physical and mental health was determined by the balance of four bodily fluids or "humors."</note>, as it is said that man is <term>sanguine</term> <note>original: *Sanguineus*; dominated by blood, characterized as cheerful or active.</note>, or <term>choleric</term> <note>original: *Cholericus*; dominated by yellow bile, characterized as irritable or ambitious.</note>, or <term>phlegmatic</term> <note>original: *Phlegmaticus*; dominated by phlegm, characterized as calm or sluggish.</note>, or <term>melancholic</term> <note>original: *Melancholicus*; dominated by black bile, characterized as somber or analytical.</note>; yet he is none of these, and this is so for many reasons. A common reason is that it is Life itself that provides what one calls <term>complexions</term>: and therefore, since it is Life that provides them and not the <term>three substances</term> <note>original: *drey Substanzen*; Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Paracelsus believed were the true fundamental components of all matter.</note>, the physician should not concern himself with them. For what exists in Life, and what pertains to and belongs to Life, is not subject to the physician: even if such <term>complexions</term> were present, they are still not for the physician to consider. For whatever passes away along with Life is not to be undertaken by a physician as part of his <term>theory</term> <note>original: *Theoric*; the systematic framework of medical knowledge</note>: the physician should well consider this within himself. For it is not only an error regarding the healthy body, but also an error regarding the sick body: for they <note>the followers of traditional medicine</note> apply it to the disease because they believe it to exist in the healthy state. But there is yet another reason: that the whole body is not capable of having such four <term>complexions</term> within a man, because they are <term>species</term> <note>original: *Species*; distinct types or categories of natural things.</note>. In no <term>species</term> is there any <term>complexion</term>, but rather the nature of its <term>substance</term>: nature is not a <term>complexion</term>. That which I say is "hot" is not its <term>complexion</term>, but its nature; it derives this from its <term>substance</term>, just like colors: but this creates neither disease nor health.

**A** Although the understanding is better, as the example goes: someone strikes another, causing a wound, or boils, or takes off a leg, or the like. Therefore, the right art is **flesh-making** <term>Incarniren: from the Latin "incarnare," meaning to heal a wound by causing new flesh to grow</term>. Do not let it trouble you whether these **flesh-forming medicines** <term>Incarnativa</term> are cold, moist, hot, or dry; if they are **flesh-formers** <term>Incarnativa</term>, you have enough; let other things be. And although it is true that wounds become hot, inflamed <note>original: "äfflig"; likely referring to a puffy or swollen state of irritation</note>, or feverish, these things are not the disease itself. It must come to this: that oil and wine are sufficient; otherwise, there is no foundation in medicine. Therefore, look to the preparation, the power, the time and hour, the property, and what is useful for it. For if you allow this to be true—that a grain of corn yields no fruit unless it be cast into the field and decays—then the other must also be true: the wound is the field, the oil and wine are the seed. Now guess what the fruit shall be?

### CHAPTER SIX

Now these things bring clearly to light the <term>Arts</term> <note>The "Arts" refers to alchemy and the study of nature's hidden powers.</note>, as they decompose and divide the living body, which is not the <term>Microcosm</term> <note>original: "Microcosmus"; the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>. That is to say, experience must occur within life. Therefore, build nothing upon this life—that which is the first—but go to the other; seek within it. That same life comes from the Arts, not to serve the soul (that is, it is not the soul's lodging in this life). In this life, the Arts are found, and the foundation is presented. For behold the weakness of the first life: if it is to enter into the operation of its <term>Arcana</term>, then the first life must...

After this intermediate life, the new life must be started, which is subject to no death, except only for the Final End, in which all things perish. <meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s discussion on the "new life" of substances. Having established that a medicine must "die" to its first form to be reborn as a potent cure, he now applies this concept of transformation—which he calls "Anatomy"—to the human body itself.</meta>

<term>Local Anatomy</term> <note>original: "Anatomey Localis"</note> is when the human being is dissected in himself, whereby it is observed what bone, flesh, and veins are, and where they lie; but that is the least of it. The second is greater, and it is this: that a new life be introduced into the human being, following the first intermediate life, into <term>Transmutation</term> <note>The process of changing a substance from one state to another, essentially an alchemical rebirth.</note>. Within this state, it is discovered what blood truly is, and what kind of <term>Sulfur</term>, <term>Mercury</term>, or <term>Salt</term> <note>These are the "Three Primes" (Tria Prima) of Paracelsian alchemy, representing the soul, spirit, and body of all substances.</note> it contains. Likewise with the heart: what kind of Sulfur, what kind of Salt, and what kind of Mercury it has; and so also with the brain, and everything in the whole body. This is now the true <term>Anatomy</term>.

This is the foundation of the beginning: in this way must the physician be born. But this birth is hard to understand, and it is a "hard saying" <note>original: "härte red"; a likely allusion to the biblical "hard saying" in John 6:60, suggesting these truths are difficult for the worldly to accept.</note> to those who will not abandon their fantasies, who trust their own heads rather than the way of truth. This is the discovery of the <term>First Matter</term> <note>original: "primae materiae"; the primal, formless essence of a substance.</note>; it is also the matter that reveals the disease to us. We must recognize this same matter so that we may also recognize the "transmuted" anatomy.

Now follows yet another anatomy, which is that of diseases, as has often been mentioned; it is not necessary to recount it here. Thus there are three anatomies that must be maintained in man: first, the **Local**, which shows the image of the human, his proportions and essence, and what belongs to him. The second demonstrates the living Sulfur, the flowing Mercury, and the <term>sharp Salt</term> <note>original: "rässe Sal"; "räss" refers to a pungent, sharp, or caustic quality.</note> in every limb. And the third instructs...

**Fever** <term>Febris</term> <note>original: "Febris"</note>: this name comes from the heat of the fever, and its heat is only a sign of the illness, and not the matter, nor the cause. Just as nettles are rightly called <term>Urtica</term> <note>original: "Urtica"; the Latin name for the stinging nettle, derived from "urere," to burn.</note> because they burn; but it is better to call them **Salt of Urine** <term>Sal Urinae</term>, for they have an **Anatomy** <term>Anatomey</term> <note>In Paracelsian medicine, "anatomy" refers to the inner chemical and spiritual composition of a thing—its "recipe"—rather than the physical dissection of a body.</note>. Therefore, **Fever** is a name that reveals its Master’s foolishness. For it is actually a **Disease of Nitre** <term>Morbus Nitri</term> and of **Burnt Sulfur** <term>Sulphuris incensi</term>. That is why it shakes the body, why it causes chills, and why it has an **Interval** <term>Intervallum</term> <note>The time between spikes in a recurring fever.</note>. And similarly, **Apoplexy** <margin>Stroke or seizure.</margin> <note>original: "Apoplexia"</note> demonstrates its own name through its Master's wisdom—that it should not be called **Apoplexy** according to the foundations of medicine, but rather **Sublimated Cachimial Mercury** <term>Mercurius Cachimialis Sublimatus</term> <note>Paracelsus suggests the stroke is caused by a "mercurial" substance that has been "sublimated" or vaporized within the body, acting as a poison to the brain.</note>. The signs are only to be used so that through them the **Body** <term>Corpus</term> and **Substance** may be recognized. He who introduces false signs and causes errs in his entire practice and in what is necessary for him. For there are many **Bodies** and their **Species** which produce heat and which produce cold; therefore the name **Fever** is false, but **Nitrous** <term>Nitreus</term> is not. This carving remains in the form of the image; but it decays and dies without the addition of the external form. He who does not eat does not grow; he who does not eat does not remain.

Now, since the growing person grows from food, and the form-maker is with him to expand his form (for he possesses a form and cannot do it without it), it follows that the nourishment of the carved image contains the form within itself, into which it enters, grows, and expands. The rain contains the tree within it, as does the **liquid of the earth** <term>Liquor terrae</term> <note>original: "Liquor terrae"; this refers to the vital, mineral-rich moisture or "sap" of the soil that Paracelsus believed carried the essential nutrients for plant growth.</note>. <meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s explanation of how nourishment functions as a restoration of the body's specific "form." **A** This is also to be considered in the same way: In all things, nourishment exists for the sake of the form alone. When summer arrives, it is a time of hunger in trees; then they wish to produce foliage, blossoms <note>original: "Blust", a word for bloom or blossom from Swabian-Swiss German</note>, fruit, and so on. What would come of it if they did not take that same form into themselves from the outside? They do not have it within themselves; for if they had it within them, they would produce it just as well when cut down as when standing in the earth. Therefore they stand in the earth so that this same form might enter into them and be forged <note>referring to the "internal smith" or Archeus mentioned on the previous page</note>, according to its property and its master—that is, its gift <note>original: "donum"</note>. Man has no need of this <note>the specific earthly rootedness of a tree</note>, for he does not produce his fruit in the same manner as a tree: regarding his "fruit," he is a different kind of creature. Know then, that all living things—for the sake of maintaining their form and because of the constant consumption of it—possess hunger and thirst, so that they may restore the image <term>bildtnuß</term> within themselves. Just as you see that fat <note>original: "Schmeer" or "Feiste", referring to grease or fatty tissue</note> increases from nourishment; where this is not provided, that part of the image wastes away. So it is with everything else. However, it is the nature of things that when this decay reaches the vital organs, death arrives quickly; for life does not remain within a fragile internal image of the common body. **A**

**A** Thus, humans grow out of humans: that is, the nourishment is the human, and it gives back the human—which is to say, the image of the same. Thus we eat ourselves. Yet, the closer a thing is to Bread, the healthier the body, and in all things there should be moderation.

## BOOK TWO
### CHAPTER ONE

**S**ince I am now to speak of the joining of the three into one <term>Body</term> <note>original: "Corpus"</note>, how they come together: In this, take for yourselves such an example. Every seed is a threefold seed: That is, a seed in which the three <term>Substances</term> <note>original: "Substanzen"; these refer to Paracelsus’s "Three Primes"—Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—which he believed were the fundamental building blocks of all matter.</note> are and grow. And just as there is only one seed present and visible, so the three appear to be only one thing. Now, every thing is united in the seed and not divided, but rather a joining into a unity. As in a nut, in which there is wood, and in which are found bark and the roots: these are three distinct <note>original: "widerwärtige"; in this context, it means "opposing" or "differing in nature" rather than the modern sense of "repulsive."</note> things, and yet they are together in one seed. 

So also is man; he is only a seed at the beginning, whose shell or hull <note>original: "schelffen"; a dialect word for a husk or pod.</note>¹) is the <term>Sperm</term> <note>original: "Sperma"; here used to describe the physical material that carries the invisible "seed" or life-force.</note>. No man has ever seen the seed itself because of its smallness and subtlety. <page-num>134</page-num>

# Of the Nature and Property of the Secret Essences
<note>original: "der Arcanen Art und Eigenschafft." In Paracelsian medicine, an "Arcanum" is the restorative healing essence or "virtue" extracted from a substance.</note>

In the same way that there is a thing that takes away life, so too is there a thing and a cause that takes away disease. You pluck a pear from the tree: now the tree is free of it. With such *names* <note>original: "Nominibus"</note> and *causes* <note>original: "Causis"</note> you must pluck away diseases; you should not dwell in the *substance* <note>original: "Substanz"</note> and *body* <note>original: "Corpus"</note> of the pear, but in the stem upon which it stands. Now note what medicine is and upon what knowledge it rests.

¶¶ Now observe these *examples* <note>original: "Exempla"</note>. You see that winter and summer alternate with one another, and how one follows the other—now cold, now warm. Expect the same within the body. However, to say that this is a "disease" is incorrect; they drive each other out. For man is subject to the summer and also to the winter. Even if he were locked away in winter within a circle of fire and did not feel the winter's cold, the winter would still exert its effect upon him—whatever it is meant to do to him—and every month [does the same]. No amount of locking away helps; just as the summer finds him too. 

Why then will the physician not recognize this and take such *celestial courses* <note>original: "cursus coelestes"; the movement of stars and planets which Paracelsus believed dictated biological rhythms.</note> into account? Instead, he acts as if nature had erred and wants to drive them out—which leads to harm rather than good. These things are also [called] diseases, just as winter is adverse to man, and the heat of summer; but in truth, they are not diseases. 

Likewise, stars run their course, making things cold and warm with their *intervening days* <note>original: "Interpolatis diebus"</note>. It is the same in *fevers* <note>original: "Febribus"</note> and the like. What are these but a cause from the heavens that moves them? Yet the physician has attributed it to the <term>microcosm</term> <note>the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note> out of his own nature and never considered the heavens; therefore, they have missed the mark. It is also true that it often happens that a person falls into a heat: it does not come from within him; it is like the sun—while it reigns, it is hot. Yet it is not innate to the one who suffers it, but rather an *accident* <note>original: "Accidens"</note> <gloss>a temporary condition or external state</gloss>.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that many conditions mistaken for internal diseases are actually external, celestial influences—like the seasons—acting upon the body. He criticizes physicians for ignoring these "celestial courses" and trying to "cure" natural astronomical rhythms.</summary>

He who turns the sun also turns away harms <note>The "harms" or "damages" here refer to diseases or celestial afflictions.</note>. Therefore, when such a heavenly heat begins, understanding is required: that the northern winds <note>original: "Borealischen Lüfft"</note> are blocked; they must be opened up, and then the constitution <note>original: "Temperament"</note> will return to how it should be. 

¶

¶ Therefore, concerning the heat of man, know where it comes from: within him are all things **celestial, terrestrial, watery, and airy** <note>original: "Coelestia Terrestria, Undosa und Aerea"</note>. Now, when all these things are unified in equal balance, it is neither cold nor warm in the body. But now, a heat must be present beyond this, which comes from the stomach; this same organ warms the body. Regarding the stomach, know that it has a mighty heat, which seethes and cooks so excellently; truly, it is not much different from external fire. However, the stomach is not alone in this: rather, every limb and organ has such a "stomach" within itself too. Therefore, in every limb there is fire, and it is the **fire of digestion** <note>original: "Ignis Digestionis"</note>. From this comes the daily heat of the body, and not from the elements that are in the body or the like. This is the primary heat that **digestion** <note>original: "Digestio"</note> provides; and the more digestion has to work, the more heat rises, and the less it works, the colder the person becomes. 

This heat causes the colors—that is, it drives forth what lies within and moves the **Mercury** <note>original: "Mercurium"; in Paracelsian chemistry, Mercury represents the principle of volatility and life-force</note> so that it blooms. But who would say, based on this blooming, "this person is of a **sanguine nature**" <note>original: "Sanguineus"; one of the four traditional temperaments characterized by blood</note>, since it is the **fire of digestion** that drives it forth? In this way, other **colors** <note>original: "colores"; used here to mean the outward signs or complexions of a patient</note> are also driven forth by daily heat, which are different in youth, different in middle age, and different in old age. But these are called **complexions** <note>original: "Complexiones"</note> <margin>See page 100.</margin>. Thus it might be said that youth is **sanguine**, middle age is **choleric**, and others are **phlegmatic** or **melancholic**, and so on. Those who speak thus forget the **heat of digestion** and the matter of the **Three Substances** <note>The "Three Substances" or "Tria Prima" are Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which Paracelsus believed composed all matter.</note> in their excellence. For every tree has its own particular **flowers** <note>original: "Flores"</note>, and so does man: and these "flowers" they call **complexions**, which is an erroneous **rule** <note>original: "Canon"; likely a jab at the "Canon of Medicine" by Avicenna or general academic medical dogma.</note>.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that bodily heat and temperaments are produced by internal "digestion" in every organ rather than the four humors. He dismisses the traditional "complexions" (sanguine, choleric, etc.) as mere outward "flowers" or symptoms of deeper chemical processes involving Mercury and the Three Substances.</summary>

❧ Therefore, understand regarding these matters: just as it is in nature regarding the growing things in the world, there are no **Degrees** <note>original: "Gradus"; refers to the Galenic system of classifying medicines by four degrees of intensity of heat, cold, moisture, or dryness.</note>, but rather **Species** <note>original: "Species"; here meaning the specific essence or unique nature of a substance.</note>. A thing should act according to its **species**, not according to **degrees**. For all things that are external do not retain the **Degree** that **Platearius** <note>Matthaeus Platearius, a 12th-century physician from the School of Salerno, famous for his book on simple medicines.</note> wrote about, or other **herbalists**, once it enters the stomach. What you have not prepared, the stomach prepares (if it is able) and it breaks all such cold, heat, and the like, and seeks out the **Arcanum** <term>Arcanum</term> <note>original: "Arcanum"; in alchemy, this is the "secret" or "incorporeal" essence of a substance that contains its true healing power, independent of its physical form.</note>. For all things "die" within the stomach: and that which dies, the physician should not take for himself <note>The physician should not rely on the dead, outward form of a plant, but on its living essence.</note>. And if the stomach does not break the substance, it is a sign of its own weakness and sickness. In such a case, the medicine is not at its best, because it cannot **putrefy** in the stomach; yet it must **putrefy**. 

Regarding the fact that some medicines for the **Pestilence** <note>The Plague.</note> are administered with heat—such as spices and the like—if they do not **putrefy**, they achieve nothing; they must **putrefy** <note>original: "fäulung"; while we usually think of rotting as bad, Paracelsus uses this term to describe the vital process of breakdown and transformation (like fermentation) necessary for the body to absorb a remedy's power.</note>. Therefore, those who do not recover through medicine are those whose stomachs did not facilitate this putrefaction. It follows then: the faster the putrefaction, the faster the health. Things that hinder putrefaction, hinder health. It is a "bad sweat" that is driven out at that time by un-putrefied medicine: it does not lead to life. From this, it is important to know that such things undertaken according to **Complexions** <note>The traditional medical theory that health depends on the balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile).</note> and **Degrees** have nothing to do with the body; for in the body, there are neither cold nor warm diseases at the root. Against whom then should a cold or warm medicine fight? The pear must be broken from the stem and felled from the tree <note>This metaphor suggests that one must strike at the root cause of a disease, detaching it from its source of growth, rather than just treating superficial symptoms like "heat."</note>. ❧

## CHAPTER TWO

**T**HEREFORE, these **Arcana** are not old things, but new things: Not an old birth, but a **rebirth**. The "old births" are the essences and forms as they stand in the world. And just as the outward form of such things is of no use to us, it must instead be broken—

He emphasizes that disease should be treated at its root rather than by balancing superficial qualities like heat or cold.</summary>

...must [die], and a new thing must become of it, otherwise it is of no use. So also there must be a losing of all old properties, cold and heat. That is to say, unless it happens that **Nightshade** <note>original: "Solatrum"; likely Black Nightshade, which was used as a cooling herb.</note> loses its coldness, it will not be a **medicine** <note>original: "Artzney".</note>. Likewise, unless it happens that **Anacardium** <note>original: "Anacardi"; the Marking Nut or Cashew fruit, known in old medicine for its intense "heat."</note> loses its heat, it will not be a medicine. This is, in summary: unless all the old nature dies away and is led into the new birth, there will be no medicine. This dying is the beginning of the separation of the evil from the good. Thus the final medicine—that is, the newborn medicine—remains without any **complexion** <note>original: "Complexion"; the traditional medical idea that health is a balance of the four "humors" or temperaments (hot, cold, moist, dry).</note> and the like, a pure **Arcanum** <term>Arcanum</term>.

Why do the errant ones say that you should not use the **degree** <note>original: "gradum"; referring to the Galenic system of classifying medicine's intensity from the 1st to 4th degree.</note> too high? That is, what you can do with the first, you should not do with the third or fourth. This is only because the stomach cannot **putrefy** <note>original: "fäulen"; to break down through a process of rot or digestion.</note> them; it is too weak for them. Otherwise, according to their own claims, it would be logical that the colder a degree is, the better, for then the **dose** <note>original: "Dosis".</note> is smaller. 

Furthermore, there is a great error in saying that this is higher in cold than that, when there is only one kind of cold in them. It would be more reasonable if they said: "This herb weighs only one **loth** <note>A traditional German unit of weight, about 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of coldness, but that one has 4 loth of coldness," if an equal weight of each were taken. From that it would follow: take the coldness as you find it, one **quintlin** <note>A small weight, about 4 grams.</note>, and give it for the heat [fever]. 

But since they feel they must have specific herbs—not **Purslane** <note>original: "Portulacam".</note>, but **Water Lily** <note>original: "Nenufar".</note>; not **Chamomile** <note>original: "Chamomillam".</note>, but **Pepper** <note>original: "Piper".</note>—this proves that they are not seeking heat or cold, but rather they seek the **Arcana** <term>Arcana</term>, even though they believe it is the **degrees** <note>original: "gradus".</note> that matter. If they knew that there was only one cold, one heat, one moisture, and one dryness, they would desist from their undertaking. But if it could be found that there were two or three different kinds of cold essences, hot essences, wet essences, or dry essences, then I would have to concede the point to them.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that true medicines are not based on Galenic "degrees" of heat or cold, but on the extraction of a pure "Arcanum" through the death of the plant's outward properties. He mocks traditional physicians for confusing the quantity of a substance with its spiritual healing essence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus's critique of traditional Galenic medicine. Following the previous page’s discussion on how the physical "degrees" and "complexions" (heat/cold) of a substance must be transformed to reach the medicinal Arcanum, he now argues that disease itself is not a lack of balance between humors, but a "rebellion" or "pride" within the three fundamental alchemical principles: Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt.</meta>

<page-num>138</page-num>

All of this has been discussed so much that a great error has been maintained regarding **the Degrees** <note>original: "de Gradibus"; the medieval system of ranking a medicine's intensity from the 1st to 4th degree.</note>, and the **constitutions of things** <note>original: "Complexiones rerum"; the traditional medical idea that health is a balance of the four qualities: hot, cold, moist, and dry.</note> are not rightly understood. They claim everything is a single thing within the four [qualities]: they have established four **Humors** <note>The traditional bodily fluids: blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile.</note>, yet it is solely the **Liquor of Mercury** <note>original: "Liquor Mercurij"; the vital, fluidic essence of the alchemical principle of Mercury, which Paracelsus believed governed the fluid parts of the body.</note>. This Mercury does not possess only four essences, but rather many hundreds of types, properties, manifestations, and the like. Furthermore, Mercury is not the sole cause; the other two principles work alongside it. For every disease exists as a "trinity" within its own **composition**. What the other two principles cause, however, is addressed in their own specific chapters.

For diseases arise just as Lucifer did in Heaven, out of their own **pride** <note>original: "hoffart"; Paracelsus uses the theological concept of "pride" as a metaphor for a natural substance rebelling against its proper function or exceeding its natural limits.</note>, which then creates all **internal wars** <note>original: "Bella intestina".</note>. Thus, when Mercury exalts itself within its Liquor—which is great and wondrous, for God created it above all other wonders—it rises up and does not remain within its proper **stations** <note>original: "staffeln"; the natural levels or boundaries assigned to a substance.</note>. This is the beginning of **discord** <note>original: "Discordanz".</note>.

It is the same with **Sulfur** and **Salt**. For when Salt exalts itself and separates itself, what is it but a consuming thing? Wherever its pride lies, there it gnaws and eats. From this eating and gnawing arise **ulcerations** <gloss>1) Suppurations, sores.</gloss>, **cancer** <gloss>2) Cancerous ulcers.</gloss>, **gangrene**, and so on. If Salt remained within its stations, the human body would never be broken open by sores. When Sulfur enters into its pride, it melts the body like snow in the sun. And Mercury can become so heightened in its **subtlety** <note>original: "Subtilitåt"; a state of extreme refinement or volatility.</note> that it climbs too high and thereby causes death, due to an excessive refinement that is beyond its station. For it is ordained in human reason that it should remain in its stations without pride; likewise, Nature should remain in its office without pride. But the minds and senses of men are so varied that they forcefully break these stations.

Now, nothing in the creatures of the flesh is meant to remain eternal. Therefore, they must be pulled apart through their manifold gifts, virtues, and powers, so that they—

<summary>Paracelsus argues that disease is caused by the "pride" of the Three Primes (Mercury, Sulfur, and Salt) when they exceed their natural boundaries, rather than a mere imbalance of the four Galenic humors. Although the title speaks of the three—that is, of doing or becoming oneself, of accidents <note>symptoms or chance occurrences</note>, and of the end—nevertheless, the others are always drawn in alongside them; that is, concerning accidents. These include the accident not only of gluttony <note>original: "Füllerei"; overindulgence in food or drink</note>, but also of the <term>Elements</term> and the like. For if a disease is to be mentioned, those things that cause it must also be mentioned. Therefore, the order is maintained in that same chapter which treats such a disease, even if the book does not follow those same things. For the books remain in their <term>Theory</term> and <term>Physical Science (Physica)</term>. Meanwhile, the <term>Practices</term> are contained in their <term>Volumes (Voluminibus)</term>.

❦

# CHAPTER SEVEN

**N**ow it is no less true that, beyond all those things already mentioned, there is another kind of disease, and two of these are contained here in this chapter. One arises from the **seed of sperm** <note>original: "Samen Spermatis." In Paracelsian medicine, "sperm" refers not just to reproductive fluid, but to a primordial "seed" or formative matter from which all things grow</note>: and one from the **specific form** <note>original: "Specifica forma"; the unique essential nature or blueprint of a thing</note>: which are particularly and greatly to be noted, and distinguished from other diseases. Now you know how all things exist in the **Three Primes** <note>the fundamental alchemical substances: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> or substances, as has been said: however, there is in these things a particular incidental growth that does not concern the matters treated until now, and it is such: there are things that cause sweating, that purge <note>original: "larieren," likely a variant of "laxieren," to act as a laxative</note>, that burn, and the like. All these things are to be highly esteemed: for they are called <term>Specific Illnesses (Aegritudines Specificae)</term> <note>diseases that have a unique, individual character rather than a general humoral cause</note>. They do not arise from the aforementioned causes <note>original: "Cauſis"</note>, but rather they are innate; they are of such a nature that one person sweats in this way, another is loose <note>lax</note> in that way, one thus, and another so.

¶ Now, regarding the **sperm** <note>original: "Spermate"</note>, know that many more generations <note>acts of creation or manifestations</note> occur than are discovered or attributed to other things out of a lack of understanding. For <term>Camphor (Camphora)</term> <margin>Flammable, volatile resin from the camphor tree. Thyme, for example, also contains camphor.</margin> proves this, as does <term>Spermaceti (Sperma coeti)</term> <margin>Literally "whale seed." Note: the source footnote links "coetus" to a crowd or multitude, but in a medical context it refers to the waxy substance from a sperm whale.</margin> and others besides. From this are caused the diseases of the **bladder** <margin>bladder</margin> and **kidneys**. For although it is true that <term>Tartar (Tartarus)</term> <margin>Literally "wine-stone." Used here metaphorically: just as tartar deposits settle in wine barrels, stone formations settle in humans.</margin> is the stone—that is, it is the material of the stone—yet without this [spermatic] kind, it never becomes a stone. The cold of the sperm congeals it, or else the <term>sweat-inducing (Diaphoretica)</term> <margin>means for inducing sweat</margin> heat of the sperm [coagulates it]; that would then be coagulated. Such heat or cold is not to be understood in the way described above, but rather that the seed of sperm has its own particular **anatomy** <note>original: "Anatomey"</note> and **physics** <note>original: "Phyſicam"</note> in its distribution, as described above: and in the same way as described above, in all...

<summary>Paracelsus introduces two new categories of disease: those arising from "sperm" (formative seeds) and those from "specific forms." He explains how these forces, rather than just elemental imbalances, lead to conditions like kidney stones and specific bodily reactions like sweating.</summary>

...just as is to be understood here. Whatever further special knowledge is necessary will be presented in its respective chapters.

**N**ow this is a special chapter: for in this way it also distinguishes itself from other diseases. What is innate <note>literally "born-in" or congenital</note> cannot be removed from the root. This is what is innate: the <term>Specific Nature (Specifica)</term> <note>the unique, essential properties or "blueprint" of a substance</note> and the **Seed** <term>(Sperma)</term> <note>original: "Sperma." In this context, it refers to the primordial formative power, not just reproductive fluid</note>; that is its nature. Therefore, the root must retain its growth. 

However, it is *not* truly innate if someone were born blind; for although he does not have sight, it is nevertheless within him, but not in its proper place. This is what makes him blind, and he appears to be born blind, even though he carries sight within him. It is just as if someone has six fingers on one hand and four on the other, or if they were not in their proper places: no experienced physician may say that such a blind person cannot be helped. Instead, nature is great and wonderful; as long as the potential is there, it can be brought to where it belongs. 

Yet this [restoration] cannot be done with the fingers: for those are the **Physical Substance of the Body** <term>(Corporis Substantia)</term>, whereas this [sight] is a "wind" <note>an intangible, spirit-like vital force</note> that has no body. Therefore, it can be moved <note>pushed or adjusted</note>, which a displaced physical body does not allow. 

But it is not so with the things taken up here in this chapter: rather, these are innate things, like the hardness of iron or the color of chalk. In this manner, it should be noted that they are received as they befall us: just as no one can hinder or prevent snow from falling, but one can certainly ensure that it does no harm to the human being. Therefore, regarding the **Seed** <term>(Sperma)</term>, because it is the <term>Primordial Matter (Limbus)</term> <note>the "Great Limbus" was Paracelsus's term for the reservoir of all potential life and matter</note> and is within the **Four Elements**, know that it possesses such power:

**T**hese powers are rightly called <term>Impressions (Impressiones)</term> <margin>Impressions, Influences</margin>, named thus by man: for they are indeed impressions. Now, note an error in **astronomy** <note>at this time, astronomy and astrology were deeply intertwined</note> regarding this matter, which is as follows: it is said that an <term>Impression (Impressio)</term> must come from the Heavens, but that is not the case.

<summary>Paracelsus distinguishes between physical birth defects and "displaced" vital spirits, arguing that the latter can be cured by a physician. ...just as it is to be understood here.

For the heavens impress nothing upon us <note>The author is rejecting the idea that the stars or planets "stamp" traits onto humans at birth.</note>: we have the image made within us by the hand of God. However we may exist in that image, it is—without any intermediary—the work and carving of God’s hand in all its limbs. He who says, "Man has an **Inclination** toward **Mars**, **Saturn**, the **Moon**, etc.," or "he must have stolen [because of his stars]": that is a great error and a hypocrisy. It is spoken more justly to say, "**Mars** follows after man, for man is more than **Mars** or other planets." 

But he who recognizes the heavens and knows man does not say such things. Instead, he might well say, "Man is so noble before God, and so highly intended by God, that his image is portrayed <note>original: "abcontrafeth," meaning depicted, modeled, or sketched as a counterpart.</note> in the heavens, with all his actions and omissions, good and evil." And although they realize this error in part, for which reason they say, "**They do not compel**" <note>original: "Non necessitant." ### CHAPTER EIGHT

**N**OW, above all this, there is an invisible body in man that is not placed within the three **Substances** <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which he believed made up all physical matter.</note>. That is, man has a body that does not come from the **Limbus**. For this reason, it is not subject to the physician; it takes its origin from the breath of God. And just as every breath or puff of air is nothing in our hands, so too is that same body nothing before our eyes. Although I must here present an argument that should be attributed to me as a physician, and accepted in such a sense as far as **Philosophy** <note>original: "Philosophy"; here meaning the study of the nature of man and the universe.</note> demonstrates concerning man, which is this: As we have in the Scripture, that we will arise on the Last Day in our body, and there give an account for our misdeeds. Now, the body that has sinned is the one that is nothing before our eyes; therefore, it is to be presumed that this same body will arise there. For we shall not give account for our bodily illnesses, health, and the like, which concerned it—but rather for the things that have come from the heart, which concern only the Per- <note>The text breaks off at the catchword "Men-", likely leading to "Mensch" (Person/Man).</note>

## Conclusion to Dr. J. v. W. <note>Joachim von Watt, also known as Vadianus (1484–1551), was a Swiss humanist, physician, and reformer to whom Paracelsus dedicated this work.</note>

**T**HUS I could not refrain, most learned Mr. von Watt, from presenting the First Book of my Paramiric works: in which I have been diligent day and night, working to instruct the <term>students of medical matters<note>original: "Auditores rei Medicae"</note></term> with such an explanation that more fruit will arise from this than might be expected. For some, this might lead to pride; for others, to a fit of rage; for a third group, to a lack of understanding. But it is true that everyone judges <term>Theophrastus<note>Paracelsus’s given name was Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim. He often referred to himself in the third person to emphasize his authority.</note></term> according to their own ability. He who is corrupted in <term>philosophy<note>To Paracelsus, "Philosophy" was not just abstract thought but the study of the invisible forces of nature.</note></term> shall have no place in this <term>monarchy<note>Paracelsus used the term "monarchy" to describe the supreme, sovereign domain of true medical knowledge.</note></term>. He who is a <term>humoralist<note>original: "Humorist"; a follower of the traditional Galenic medicine which believed disease was caused by an imbalance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile). Paracelsus famously rejected this theory.</note></term> in medicine does not praise Theophrastus. He who is lost in <term>astronomy<note>Here referring to those who misunderstand the influence of the stars on human health.</note></term> accepts nothing of what I say. They say my <term>physics<note>original: "Physica"</note></term>, my <term>study of meteors<note>original: "Meteorica"</note></term>, my <term>theory<note>original: "Theorica"</note></term>, and my <term>practice<note>original: "Practica"</note></term> are strange, new, marvelous, and unheard of. But how can I not be strange to one who has never walked in the sun? I am not frightened by the crowd of <term>Aristotle<note>The ancient Greek philosopher whose logic and natural science were the standard for medieval universities.</note></term>, nor of <term>Ptolemy<note>The ancient authority on astronomy and geography.</note></term>, nor of <term>Avicenna<note>A Persian physician whose "Canon of Medicine" was the primary medical textbook of the era; Paracelsus famously burned his books in public.</note></term>. Instead, I am frightened by the ill-will that is placed so often in my path, and by the untimely laws, customs, and orders—as they call them—of <term>jurisprudence<note>original: "Iurisprudentiae"; Paracelsus often complained that legal and academic regulations stifled true medical innovation.</note></term>. To him whom the gifts are given, the gift belongs. He who is not called, I have no duty to call. But may God be with us, our protector and sustainer into eternity.

->Farewell<-

# ON THE ORIGIN AND CAUSE OF DISEASES OF BOTH PROFESSIONS <note>original: "De Morborum Utriusque Professionis Origine et Causa." The "both professions" refers to the dual nature of man—the physical and the spiritual—and the corresponding need for two types of healing.</note>

## BY AUREOLUS THEOPHRASTUS PARACELSUS TO MR. JOACHIM VADIANUS, PHYSICIAN <note>original: "Aureoli Theophrasti Paracelsi ad D. Joachimum Vadianum Medicum." Joachim von Watt, known as Vadianus (1484–1551), was a Swiss scholar and the reformer of St. Gallen.</note>

### THE THIRD BOOK OF THE PARAMIRUM <note>original: "Liber Tertius Paramiri." The Paramirum is one of Paracelsus's foundational works on the causes of disease.</note>

### To the Reader

**ALTHOUGH** the time of rest is withheld from me, experienced reader, and there is no one who wishes to grant it, I cannot overlook the opportunity, since I have before me the venerable and highly learned Mr. Joachim von Watt, Doctor of Medicine, Mayor and <term>City Physician</term> <note>original: "Physicum." A "Physicus" was an officially appointed municipal doctor responsible for public health.</note> of the city of St. Gallen, to present—as is only right and proper—a general theory of <term>both medicines</term> <note>Likely referring to the medicine of the "visible" body and the "invisible" or spiritual body.</note> based on my experience. And although I began such a work in Basel with no small diligence and was in good hope of reaping fruit from it, the winds are smoke and storm <note>original: "räß," meaning raging or stormy. Paracelsus uses this metaphor to describe the academic hostility he faced in Basel.</note> (whenever the truth begins to rise) to drive away the professors. Yet I have always hoped that whoever loves the soul would also love the body: he who spares the soul, he [also spares the body...]

<summary>Paracelsus begins the third book of his Paramirum with a dedication to the Swiss humanist Joachim Vadianus, lamenting the professional opposition he faced in Basel while asserting the necessity of a unified theory for both physical and spiritual health.</summary>

<keywords>Paracelsus, Joachim Vadianus, St. Gallen, Basel, medical theory, soul and body, medical reform, early modern medicine</keywords>

[it] spared not even the body, in which I intended to perform no small service. But among such a multitude, my work was split apart; that was a harsh wind to me. Therefore, reader, be attentive: do not judge the first, the second, or the third chapter, but wait until the end, and weigh with your own experience that which I encompass in these few pages. Do not be horrified by those whom I attack: measure and consider it without favor or friendship, in an equal balance. For there will yet more books follow (by God's <term>providence</term> <note>original: "Verhängnuß." In this context, it refers to divine ordainment or the unfolding of destiny.</note>), built upon this foundation, which will delight you even more, so that you may recognize and learn from them.

Given at St. Gallen on the 15th day of March, in the 3rd year <note>likely referring to 1531, or the third year of his travels following his departure from the University of Basel.</note>.

# THEOPHRASTUS VON HOHENHEIM
## ON THE CAUSE AND ORIGIN OF DISEASES

### BOOK THREE

### FIRST TREATISE

**W**ho among the philosophers of natural things would not laugh when they observe and see that physicians have omitted and forgotten the most necessary parts which are found and grounded in <term>philosophy</term> <note>In Paracelsus’s view, "philosophy" is not just abstract logic, but the deep study and understanding of the inner workings of nature.</note>, and which also apply here in medicine to many illnesses and pains? But they themselves skip over these things, and set their <term>fish-traps</term> <note>original: "Fiſchbåren." A metaphor for setting traps to catch money from patients, rather than seeking truth.</note> only to take in money and to dispute with peasants and laymen. Yet, they should first of all hold disputes with the philosophers regarding their <term>subjects</term> <note>original: "Subiecten" / "subiectum." In scholastic and Paracelsian terms, this refers to the underlying substance or the "matter" being acted upon—in this case, the human body and the nature of the disease itself.</note>; for if they are not at one with philosophy, they do not even know what their subject actually is. Now behold, if they are not at one with the philosophers and do not engage in dispute with them, then everything they do is flawed and in vain. ❧

❧ It is a coarse thing in a physician who calls himself a physician yet is empty of philosophy and does not know it. What <term>error</term> <note>original: "Irrſal." A term for a wandering away from the truth or a state of confusion.</note> has arisen from this will be easy for you to recognize from what follows. ❧

❧ Although a book has already been set down concerning the cause and origin of diseases, yet there is another one here...

<summary>Paracelsus begins his third book by critiquing physicians who prioritize profit and arguing with laypeople over the fundamental study of natural philosophy. He asserts that a physician without a philosophical understanding of nature cannot truly understand the "subject" of their own medical practice.</summary>
<keywords>natural philosophy, medical ethics, medical theory, scholasticism, Paracelsus, nature of disease</keywords>

and that which also causes and provides [diseases], and these are manifold. You should understand them in this way and let yourself be well-instructed in <term>philosophy</term> therein, namely, how all things have three <term>substances</term> <note>Paracelsus refers here to his "Tria Prima"—Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury—which he believed were the fundamental building blocks of all matter.</note>. Now, these same three things have with them an <term>excretion</term> <gloss>emptying</gloss> <note>original Latin: "egestion"; German gloss: "Ausleerung."</note>, dung, and impurity; for there is nothing that serves as nourishment that does not also have within it the filth or dung of its own digestion. This is to be understood more significantly in general: All things that exist and grow have within them their own <term>manure</term> <gloss>manure</gloss> <note>original Latin: "stercus"; German gloss: "Mist."</note> or <term>filth</term> <gloss>from the Latin for feces or rubbish</gloss> <note>original Latin: "merdam"; German gloss: "Kot, Unrat."</note>. Just as a human being has these within himself, so too does every individual thing have them for itself. ❦

❦ Thus, it was said in the beginning concerning the three first substances of the body; but this further shows the diseases of these three first [substances]—their excretion and dung—and what that same filth and dung causes within us. You should understand and experience this, and not let yourself be horrified that the ancients were silent about it. The fault lies in the fact that they understood nothing in any of these matters; why then would they have done any better here? ❦

❦ Therefore, I will now further entrust to <term>philosophy</term> that which you should understand here, namely, that you should know: All things grow and live, therefore they must have eaten; and because they must eat, they must have a stomach and that same power [of digestion]. From this, it follows that they eat both pure and impure things, just as humans do. But they do not have <term>cleansing organs</term> <note>original Latin: "emunctoria." In early medicine, these were the parts of the body—like the armpits, behind the ears, or the groin—where waste was thought to be expelled.</note> like humans do; what they eat remains in them. The good separates from the bad and goes into the nourishment of that thing; the bad leaves that <term>anatomy</term> <note>Paracelsus uses "anatomy" here not to mean a dissected body, but the internal structural blueprint and functional arrangement of a substance.</note> and has its own separate anatomy, and it also remains within the same thing. Thus, the dung remains in the thing along with the <term>nourishment</term> <note>original Latin: "nutrimentum."</note>. Now, concerning the dung that is thus within the nourishment, I will speak of it, but I will entrust the greater part of it to philosophy. ❦

<summary>Paracelsus explains that all living things contain three primary substances which produce waste (dung) during digestion. He argues that unlike humans, many things lack specific organs to expel this waste, causing it to remain within their internal "anatomy."</summary>

⸿ Now, concerning the matter at hand, you should know that such <term>nourishment</term> <note>original Latin: "nutriment"</note> and <term>waste</term> <note>original Latin: "stercus," often meaning dung or excrement</note> are consumed and drunk together by human beings. From this it follows that the <term>nature</term> <note>In Paracelsian thought, "Nature" refers to the internal "Archaeus" or alchemist that manages the body's functions.</note> of the human separates them from one another and does not let them remain as one thing. Rather, because it is two-fold, it must also become two things: that is, the nature and the <term>waste</term>. Yet, although this is so, the human <term>stomach</term> does not separate these two. For it separates only its own <term>waste</term> from what is pure—and not the <term>waste</term> of the natural things themselves—but rather, that same <term>waste</term> is so closely bound to the <term>nourishment</term> that the stomach, in its official duty, cannot separate the two. Instead, it entrusts this to the <term>subtle stomach</term> <note>Paracelsus viewed individual organs as smaller "stomachs" that further refined nutrients.</note> found in the <term>mesenteric veins</term> <note>original: "meseraicis"</note>, in the <term>liver</term> <note>original: "hepate"</note>, in the <term>kidneys</term> <note>original: "renibus"</note>, in the <term>bladder</term> <note>original: "vesica"</note>, in the <term>intestines</term>, and such. In those same "stomachs," such <term>wastes</term> <note>original: "stercora"</note> are separated. Therefore, you should know that our stomach—that is, the first stomach, hanging from the <term>gullet</term> <note>original German: "Halßrohr," literally "neck-pipe" or esophagus</note>—only separates that which decays from that which does not decay, and that which breaks down from that which does not break down. Now, nothing breaks down except that which is not flesh, marrow, or bone. Therefore, whatever is not "the human" is <term>filth</term> <note>original German: "koth"</note>; whatever is "the human" is not <term>filth</term>. Now, the <term>wastes</term> of things are not the <term>filth</term> of the human, but rather of those very things; thus they are also not breakable, nor are they "human." For this reason, they remain in the human, and are in the human, and because of this, they are so "boiling" <note>This likely refers to a state of metabolic or chemical activity that causes inflammation or "heat" in the body if not properly expelled.</note>. ⸿

⸿ Thus, because there lies within the human that which should not lie within them—which is not their own <term>waste</term>, and is not the human themselves, but the <term>waste</term> of natural things (that is, of food and drink) in the manner presented before—it is appropriate to write about what those same <term>nourishments</term> do and how they act within the body. And although it is strange and unusual, that is only due to the inexperience of those who wonder at it. Now, such <term>diseases</term> <note>original German: "kranckheiten"</note> that arise in this way are different diseases than those mentioned...

<summary>Paracelsus describes the digestive process as a series of separations performed by "subtle stomachs" (organs like the liver and kidneys) which must extract the pure nourishment from the inherent waste found in food. He explains that diseases arise when this external waste is not properly separated and remains active or "boiling" within the body.</summary>

is in the first book. Although it is true that all <term>waste</term> <note>original Latin: "stercora"</note> exists and stands within the three <term>substances</term> <note>The "Tria Prima" of Paracelsus: Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury, which he believed made up all matter.</note> just as much as everything else: nonetheless, they are separated from the others, just as a human is separated from <term>excrement</term> <note>original German: "koth," referring to dung, filth, or waste</note>, as will be mentioned in the appropriate places. Thus, the <term>diseases</term> <note>original: "Kranckheiten"</note> also separate themselves from one another—those which arise from the human, and those which arise from the <term>excrement</term>—with the aforementioned distinction: so that there is a completely different and special understanding required for these <term>diseases of the waste</term>.

And although the ancient <term>writers</term> <note>original: "Scribenten," referring to classical medical authorities like Galen.</note> and their following heavily blame <term>choller</term>, <term>phlegm</term>, and <term>melancholy</term> in such matters: yet because it is unfathomable, why should any attention be paid to that? They do not consider, when they write of these things, the foundation of <term>Philosophy</term> <note>In this context, "Philosophy" refers to "Natural Philosophy," the study of how nature and the physical world actually function.</note>; thus, they cannot find a place or position for their <term>humors</term> <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that traditional medicine believed controlled health.</note>. These <term>diseases</term> are stone and sand, glue and clay. Now tell me of your <term>humors</term>: how can they become stones, sand, clay, or glue, when they were not these things to begin with? If a stone, or sand, or clay, or glue is to form in a human, it must be present in that from which it comes: if it is not in the source, then that which it is not cannot be born from it. And although an explanation has been introduced into these matters outside of those same four <term>humors</term>: yet, just as they justify it with other reasons, so they do with this: that is, the cause of the ailments. If they were <term>philosophers</term> instead of <note>original: "für," used here as "instead of"</note> poets, and <term>anatomists</term> instead of <term>followers of the Canon</term> <note>original: "Canonicisten," those who swear by the "Canon of Medicine" by the Persian physician Avicenna.</note>, and <term>truth-tellers</term> <note>original Latin: "Veraces"</note> and not <term>buffoons</term> <note>original Latin: "nugatores"</note>, then...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that diseases like kidney stones or gout (sand/clay) cannot be caused by the four humors because those humors do not contain stony properties. ...they would build correctly in those things in such diseases outside of human type and nature. [Symbol] [Symbol] So you should understand it thus: that the **body** <note>original: "Corpus"</note> which gives and makes this disease is of four kinds: a stone, a sand or grit, a clay, a loam. These four are the four **wastes** <note>original: "stercora"</note> of natural things. And all the **nutrients** <note>original: "nutrimenta"</note> that natural things eat and drink have these four types—which is either a stone, or a grit, a clay, or a loam—but in the end, it is all **coagulation** <note>original: "Coagulatio"</note>; that is the **final state** <note>original: "ultimum esse"</note>. That is, in the end, everything becomes a stone, which is **coagulation**. Now it is first to be proven <gloss>to be made true</gloss> that these **wastes** have their **ultimate matter** <note>original: "ultimam materiam"</note> in stone, and it is so. Human **wastes** have **decay** <note>original: "putrefactionem"</note> in their **ultimate matter**; the **ultimate matter** of natural things is **coagulation**. This is now the counter-play against each other: for the reason is that human **digestion** <note>original: "Digestia"</note> has its **organs of excretion** <note>original: "Emunctoria"; refers to the body's natural channels for waste elimination, like the pores or the bowels.</note>. Therefore, what goes out from there goes out through decay; this decay itself creates its own **power of expulsion** <note>original: "virtutem expulsivam"</note>. For the **power of expulsion** is in the filth and dung, not in the human nature or property. But now in natural things, this [expulsive power] is not present; therefore, as they are such, they are **coagulative** <note>original: "Coagulativa"</note>, and for this reason: their **nutrients** take from their own kind. For **Plantain** <gloss>original Latin: Plantago; Wegerich</gloss> eats **Plantain**, **Sweet Flag** <gloss>original Latin: Acorus; Kalmus</gloss> eats **Sweet Flag**, and so on with the others. Now, at the beginning of this **nutrition** <note>original: "Nutrition"</note>, all things are in **coagulation**, and this same thing **dissolves** <note>original: "resolvirt"</note> into a nutrient. Therefore, that which is not digested into that by which it is eaten, goes back into its **coagulation** from which it came. For this **dissolution** <note>original: "Resolutio"</note> must come out of the coagulation, which is twofold: that which never coagulates again, and that which coagulates again. That which never coagulates again is **nourishment** <note>original: "nutrimentum"</note>; that which coagulates is **waste** <note>original: "stercus"</note>. For in the same way as in a human, whatever is not the human, that same thing...

<summary>Paracelsus explains that natural waste products tend toward "coagulation" (solidification into stone or clay), whereas human waste is characterized by "putrefaction" (decay). He argues that minerals and plants consume their own kind and that disease occurs when waste products revert to their solid, coagulated state within the body.</summary>

He who prepares wood makes **stony deposits** <term>Duelech: a term coined by Paracelsus to describe tartar or stone-like calcifications that form inside the body</term> out of it; he who prepares the herb makes **alabaster** out of it, and the like. 

These are the **ultimate matters of the waste of natural things** <note>original: "ultimae materiae stercoris rerum naturalium"</note>. For truly, if a thing burns, it has **Sulphur** in it; if it yields ash, it has **Salt** in it; if it yields smoke, it has **Mercury** in it. <note>These three—Sulphur, Salt, and Mercury—are known as the "Tria Prima," the three primary principles Paracelsus believed made up all material things.</note> Since it has these three, it also has its excrements in like manner: not burning, but stony; not in smoke, but **coagulated**; not in salt, but in the form. That is to say: wood gives ash, ash gives salt, salt gives **stone** <note>original: "lapidem"</note>. 

Thus know also that the **Inner Artisan** <term>Mechanicus: refers to the 'Archeus,' an internal alchemist or vital force that Paracelsus believed resided in the stomach to separate useful nutrients from waste</term> is in the body, who brings it to this point and reveals its **ultimate matter** within the body. Which peasant sees oil in wood? None. Which sees water in stone? None, except for the physician. Thus he must search again for that which is not [apparent]...

...that it is there; that is, wood in oil, a stone in water: this is now **learned, shrewd philosophy** <note>original: *Philosophia adepta sagax*; Paracelsus uses this term to describe a philosophy based on practical experience and keen observation of nature.</note>.

As stated above, there are four **categories** <note>original: *genera*</note>: **Stone** <note>original: *Calculus*; specifically bladder or kidney stones</note>, **Sand** <note>original: *Arena*</note>, **Clay** <note>original: *Bolus*; a reddish, fatty type of clay</note>, and **Slime** <note>original: *Viscus*; a tough or viscous mucus</note>. These four things must be sought within the body—that is, in nourishment, for nourishment is the body. When they enter the body, they are born there according to the **Spirit** <note>original: *Spiritus*</note> that is present, which is the **Mechanic** <note>original: *Mechanicus*</note> in that place—that is, the smith of such things. Now, this book is titled according to its category as **On Tartar** <note>original: *de Tartaro*</note>, which is appropriate. Therefore, Tartar is, or is called, stone, sand, clay, slime, and so on. Following this is the book on Tartar, explaining the distinctions and **species** <note>original: *speciebus*</note> by which it is to be understood.

Thus it has been concluded so far that **Tartar** is solely the **waste** <note>original: *Excrementum*</note> of food and drink itself, which is **solidified** <note>original: *coagulirt*</note> within man by his **spirits** in such a way: if they are not mixed with their own expelling power and driven out in that mixture, then what follows arises from it. Thus we eat and drink **Tartar**, and when it enters us, unless it is mixed into our **waste** and expelled with that same pile, it remains in the body. From this, many kinds of diseases arise in various ways, which until now have been kept secret by physicians, both ancient and modern—not out of unfaithfulness or spite, but out of ignorance and lack of understanding.

But if during cooking this substance is removed, it is broken down so that such material leaves through other **waste products** <note>original: *Excrementen*</note> which otherwise would have clung [to the body].

Thus, this **pitch** <note>original: *Bitumen*</note>, **viscosity** <note>original: *Viscus*</note>, **slime** <gloss>original: *mucilago*; a thick, gluey substance</gloss>, and **glue** <gloss>original: *gluten*; a sticky moisture</gloss> of **legumes** <term>legumina: plants like peas, beans, and lentils</term> is nothing other than **fecal matter** <note>original: *materia stercorum*</note>, which—as stated above—turns into stone and sand in the body when it reaches its **ultimate matter**.

In the same way, know also about **dairy products** <note>original: *Lacticiniis*</note>; these produce **clay-like matter** <note>original: *Bolarem materiam*</note>, which is clayey <gloss>original: *Lettisch*; from "Letten," an old term for clay or loam</gloss>. Understand by this that all **dairy products** <note>original: *Lacticinia*</note> contain a **clay-lump** <gloss>original: *bolum*</gloss> within them; from this **clay-lump** comes **Tartar**, unless it is expelled with the **waste products**. Likewise, meat also contains this **clay-lump**, as do fish.

**A** Thus, know that **legumes** produce their **feces** in a slimy form, while fish, meat, and **dairy products** produce their **feces** in a clay-like or "bolary" form. From these two, understand the two types of **feces**; otherwise, no other types of **Tartar** arise from our food except for the **Tartar of clay** <note>original: *Tartarum boli*</note> and the **Tartar of slime** <note>original: *Tartarum visci*</note>, along with their various **species** <note>original: *speciebus*</note>, depending on how **legumes**, **meats** <note>original: *carnes*</note>, **grains** <note>original: *frumenta*</note>, **herbs**, and so on, are separated and divided. For **stalks** <gloss>original: *caules*; the stems of herbaceous plants</gloss>, **roots**, and **grains** are included and understood within the category of **legumes**.

Therefore, a physician prescribing a diet for such diseases should arrange the preparation of food so that these **tartaric kinds** and **excrements** are mixed into the **digestive processes** <gloss>original: *putrefactiones*</gloss> and **waste products** of the stomach and its expelling forces. Otherwise, the regimen and **diet** <note>original: *diaeta*</note> cannot be established in any other way than through...

This does not happen in solid foods, but only in drinks, which contain so many <term>waste products</term> <note>original: *Excremente*</note> and are too weak to hold onto them; thus, the deposits fall away from them.

This same nourishment must be taken according to how it enters the stomach, as is stated in its **chapters**. Although this separation [of waste] rarely happens perfectly: for the reason that the urine over-moistens it, so that the **Tartar** <term>Tartarus: in Paracelsian medicine, this refers to stony or calcified deposits formed when the body's "internal alchemist" fails to separate waste from nourishment</term> flows out of these same kidneys and cannot be separated from their waste <note>original: *Excrementen*</note>, yet it [the kidney] is just as prepared for this as the other limbs. Now the kidneys also take in their nourishment according to the distribution and that same **anatomy** which occurs within the human being—the "inner man" who consumes the nourishment provided to the person. This is distributed to each part as it is entitled, along with those same **wastes** <note>original: *excrementis*</note> that otherwise can never be separated except through the specific limb where they reside. Thus the kidneys also have their own particular waste, just like all others.

This waste mixes with the urine and passes out with it, and it is the **Sediment** <note>original: *Hypostasis*</note> ²): Therefore, the sediment allows one to judge the kidneys in their ailments, for it is their waste, and it separates itself from the urine into its own part, like oil and water, which also do not allow themselves to be mixed. And just as the oil floats on top and the water stays below, so is the property of the sediment: to divide itself in the middle, or similarly, from the top down to the bottom, according to how well it is expelled. Now, there is an art to separating the sediment from the urine, so that the sediment is caught in a separate vessel and the urine separately. Therefore, based on this, he who is able to do so sees the waste of the kidneys thoroughly: and...

<margin>1) Madness. 2) Sediment of the urine.</margin>

...one sees thereby, in the preparation and separation of that same thing, the **ultimate matter** <term>Ultima Materia: the final form of a substance after all processing; here, the final state of stones or calcified deposits in the body</term> of the stones.

They have brought things to such a pass that all people flee from medicine and consider it knavery and fraud <note>original: *Büberey und Beſcheiſſerey*</note>.

Thus they have deceived the people with their arts, so that a common peasant—or even a Jew <note>In the 16th century, Jewish healers and folk practitioners were often preferred over university-trained doctors because they relied on practical experience rather than the rigid theories of Galen or Avicenna</note>—has more credibility than they do. Is it not a vice and a shame that a city physician should reside in a town with a salary <note>original: *Proviſion*</note>, yet the sick flee from him? He cannot help them, must leave them lying there, while others who have not studied medicine help them? Is that an honor? It is shameful even to speak of it. This happens because your learning is worth nothing: you are "poets," practicing medicine poetically <note>Paracelsus uses "poets" as a derogatory term for doctors who rely on imagination, rhetoric, and book-learning rather than the "light of nature" and chemical reality</note>. And no matter how many of you there were, you would not know how to defend your own doctors, nor they you. Only long habit, tradition, and the order of the universities <note>original: *Hohenſchulen*</note> sustain you, where nothing but hypocrites <note>original: *Gleißner*</note> and scribes <note>original: *Schreiber*</note> are raised. A "scribe" is one who presents a recipe but heals no one; thus he is a doctor of writing, but not of healing.

So you are scribes, which is to say hypocrites, and you have a particular sect like the Pharisees; for no one is allowed to speak against your business. You behave just like the monastic orders, who do not know what is white or black. Is it not a shame that you have never [extracted] from the sediment <note>original: *Hypostaſi*</note>...

Now it is the case that, if it exceeds its proper weight, then it **sweats it out**: That which sweats out through the capsule, however, is airy and not heavy, but of a light spirit.

Tartar is there, in the form that it is, where the **prime matter** <note>original: *prima materia*; the fundamental, unformed base of a substance</note> lies: And so **Tartar** <note>original: *Tartarus*</note> generates itself within the **capsule** <note>original: *Capsula*; the pericardium, or the sac surrounding the heart</note> in which the heart lies. No one is there to contradict them, so these fools remain **Doctors** of medicine, and their own hearts are full of these foolish arts—they are more than mere fools. But if one were to examine them rightly and find the lack of order in them, they would perhaps be paid with beatings, or be whipped out of town, or even worse. These are the murderers of whom **God’s Commandment** says, "thou shalt not kill." Therefore, learn so that you kill no one, or else go back to plowing the fields. For they, just as much as you, are handed over to the executioner. Therefore, one thief might try to excuse himself by pointing to another. The blind shall fall together.
