¶ Now you should also know in this way about the spleen, which likewise contains the material of the stone within its waste products.

¶ Now it is said that the spleen purges itself through the eyes: this is not found to be true. For wherever an outlet of an <term>Emunctory</term> <note>Emunctory: an organ or duct that carries off waste from the body, such as the pores, kidneys, or bowels.</note> is located, that is where its health is to be regained. Just as the stomach has its emunctory through the <term>Monoculum</term> <note>original: *Monoculum*; in early anatomy, this often referred to the cecum or "blind gut."</note>: if something is lacking in it, one drives it out from there, and it leaves. But if that does not happen, the stomach must endure its sickness. The same applies to the urine in its channels. 

If the spleen were to have its emunctory through the eyes, we would also need medicines that cause weeping, so that the spleen’s diseases—<term>quartan fever</term> <note>original: *quartana*; a fever that recurs every four days, traditionally associated with the spleen.</note>, <term>obstruction</term> <note>original: *opilatio*; a medical term for a blockage or clogging of the internal organs.</note>, and so on—would pass out and be separated through that path. However, since the spleen does not expel its sickness through weeping, nor the liver through laughter, these are not emunctories; rather, it is something else that weeps and something else that laughs. 

Therefore, it is a gross error among the doctors that they have forgotten that all emunctories have specific medicines: <term>Colocynth</term> <note>A bitter cucumber used as a powerful purgative.</note> for the intestines, <term>Esula</term> <note>Spurge, a plant whose sap was used as a drastic purge.</note> for the mouth of the stomach, <term>Nipalen</term> <note>Likely *Nepeta* (catnip) or a related herbal preparation.</note> and <term>Precipitate</term> <note>A chemical preparation, often a metallic oxide, used in alchemy and medicine.</note> for the liver <unclear>Pt. Mz.</unclear>, radish for the bladder, <term>Linaria</term> <note>Toadflax.</note> for the nose along with sneezing powder, peach leaves, and so with others. But for weeping, there has never been any medicine that purged the spleen's emunctory. 

Yet, as the Doctors are in all things, so they are in this. It is one of the points of their wisdom: for if quartan fever were to pass away through the eyes, they would still try to drive it through the backside, or seek to let it out another way, through sweating and the like. All of this is caused by the error they carry in anatomy, philosophy, and in the **Light of Nature**.

For you have had a long, wicked custom until now, which has produced little of use, but has certainly increased that which you should have averted. And especially so, in that you now claim the spleen cleanses itself through the eyes, or the gallbladder through the ears: for both are untrue. But you say these things because no one can prove otherwise through experience; therefore, you are believed in your lies, which are imposed by force. Where all the dismissed <term>Bachelors</term> <note>original: *Baccalaurei*; those holding the lowest academic degree.</note>, <term>Schoolmasters</term> <note>original: *Ludimagistri*.</note>, <term>Attorneys</term> <note>original: *Procuratores*.</note>, <term>Poets</term>, <term>Historians</term>, and scholars of Greek, Arabic, Chaldean, and Jewish learning sustain themselves—along with monks, nuns, executioners, harlots, and dog-killers. If you were truly Doctors, your books would surely demonstrate enough skill that no executioner could outdo you. But because your books are worth nothing, the executioner has plenty of room to out-skill and out-dispute you; that is your great failing.

## FIFTH TRACTATE

**SO** then, moving further, there is another genus of <term>Tartar</term>, namely that which exists outside of the principal organs—such as in the blood, flesh, marrow, and other such parts—as they are generally grouped together.

Now, although this is so, <term>tears</term> <note>original: *lachrymae*</note> are not to be understood as being part of this discussion! The reason is that it is not well known from where they come or how they arise in their <term>matter</term> <note>original: *materia*</note> or <term>substance</term>. For they come from both weeping and laughing, and the origin of neither is certain as to where the spring lies from which they flow. Therefore, no description of them shall be made in this place. Rather, you should know that in these matters, the blood, the marrow, and the flesh also have and give birth to their own <term>Tartar</term> <note>Paracelsus’s term for stony or calcified deposits in the body, which he believed caused various diseases.</note>. Now, we must first speak of where they put their <term>excrement</term>. Namely, it is solely the sweat that passes through the skin which is the <term>excrement of the blood</term> <note>original: *excrementum sanguinis*</note>. That which comes out of the flesh is <term>clotted blood</term> <note>original: *Cruor*; the red, coagulating part of the blood.</note>, which distills <margin>into the branching vessels</margin> into the branches. That which is in the marrow is consumed by the dryness of the bone; however, whatever is not consumed comes into the <term>hollow spaces</term> <note>original: *Concavität*</note> of the joints and <term>ligaments</term> and other such coverings.

Of these three, as they are the most common and the greatest, we must speak specifically. Whatever other <term>kinds of Tartar</term> <note>original: *Tartari generibus*</note> exist will also be included in their proper place. But now, regarding these three, take careful note: a great many diseases arise and spring from the blood which are explained as coming from many other causes—resulting in doctors acting falsely in their <term>prescriptions</term> <note>original: *Receptis*</note> and <term>cures</term> <note>original: *Curis*</note>. Therefore, observe this <term>type of Tartar</term> <note>original: *genus Tartari*</note> so that the same error may be prevented, which causes many people to be brought to their death through the arrogant misunderstanding of their physicians.

# THE FOURTH BOOK OF THE PARAMIRUM
## CONCERNING THE WOMB <note>original: *De Matrice*</note>

**N**ow, beyond all that I have said concerning the conditions of human beings, the story is not yet fully told. Paracelsus viewed the womb not just as an organ, but as a "microcosm within a microcosm" with its own unique biological and spiritual laws</note>, and concerns women alone. 🕃 Therefore, know that I speak of invisible things. For who is there who has seen in the **anatomy of the womb** <note>original: *Anatomia Matricis*</note> those things which I set forth in what follows? Therefore, in the air we may certainly "see" that which we perceive, even though we do not see it with our eyes. For the task of seeing is commanded not only to the eyes, but also to the sense of perception. ❧ That which is visible, however, is the woman; she is placed within the three **substances** <term>Substanz</term>, **Sulfur** <term>Sulphur</term>, **Salt** <term>Sal</term>, and **Mercury** <term>Mercurium</term> <note>These are the 'Tria Prima,' the three fundamental principles of Paracelsian alchemy—combustibility, stability, and fluidity—from which all physical bodies are composed.</note>, just as all **bodies** <term>Corpora</term> exist in those states. For whatever is to be used tangibly must be visible, and this is the whole body of the woman. We must speak and philosophize regarding the **ultimate matter** <term>ultima materia</term> <note>The final, realized form of a substance or the specific manifestation of a disease.</note>, so that its sovereignty may be found: for all her diseases arise from these three. That is, what the ultimate matter of the aforementioned **prime matters** <term>primae materiae</term> <note>The original, raw materials of nature before they take specific form.</note> is, that is also the prime matter of those same diseases. Therefore, it is first necessary to know that there are three substances which cause these diseases, as they befall women—knowingly and unknowingly, past, present, and even those yet to come. 

In this, it is to be noted that women are subject to all the external stars, just like men, yet within a divided **physics** <term>Physica</term> <note>The natural laws or physical constitution.</note>. In the same way as a loaf of bread lying before us is set as food for all animals: if a man eats it, it becomes human flesh; if a fish eats it, it becomes fish-flesh. Now see how these two types of flesh are distinct from one another; just as far apart is the **theory** <term>Theorica</term> of such **impressions** <term>Impression</term> <note>The 'stamping' or influence of celestial forces upon the physical body.</note>, **infections** <term>Infection</term>, and so on, to be recognized from one another. Therefore, it is right to observe this same division: since **medicine** <term>Artzney</term> and all herbs possess this distinction, so too should the physician who acts with truth and not with lies. ❧

Take this example: Imagine a case of **jaundice** <note>original: *Geelsucht*; literally "yellow-sickness."</note> in a man and one in a woman. # THE ARGUMENT
<note>original: *ARGUMENTUM*; a Latin term for a summary or the logical basis of a discourse.</note>

## Concerning the books that follow

**N**OW, to further instruct you on what will be treated hereafter: Know that there are two philosophies; likewise, there are also two paths of medicine. One is written concerning bodily illnesses; following this, the non-bodily <note>Paracelsus refers here to "spiritual" or "invisible" diseases that do not originate in the physical flesh but in the mind, soul, or celestial influences.</note> illnesses will be understood and divided into four books, explaining why they are invisible and how they shall be made visible. 

The first book encompasses the diseases that faith gives us, and as far as faith may comprehend and encompass. The second book treats the <term>impressions</term> <note>original: *impressionibus*; in Paracelsian thought, these are invisible influences or "imprints" cast upon the human being by the stars and the heavens.</note> of the hidden heaven, and in what way and form that same heaven works within us. The third book concerns the diseases of the imagination, and how the imagination may give birth to itself without any <term>matter</term> <note>original: *materia*; physical substance.</note>. After that, the fourth book concerns the secrets of natural powers which work against bodily reason through the specific properties of their own body. And thus, as these things are the work of Nature, they shall be sought here with me. 

And although one thing will be <margin>lacking</margin> <note>original: *gebresten*; the author notes that a specific section may seem to be missing.</note>, namely the book of healing, for that reason the fifth book follows after the four, in which every person will be sufficiently satisfied.

If we then have a faith, and with it we fall into evil things, which Holy Scripture in its German tongue calls "Tempting" <note>original: *Versuchen*. > "Lead us not into temptation," that is, "do not ordain temptation for us."

## How Faith Makes the Body Sick

**N**OW, why is it that I relate these things, when I have not yet touched upon my primary intention: how it happens that faith makes the body sick. For until now I have only <term>treated (original: *tractiert*); discussed or examined in a scholarly or medical manner</term> the powers and strength of faith. But now, concerning another point of misuse, it is as follows.

...in the same way as a physician, who has good medicines at his disposal: depending on what kind of person he is, he may act accordingly. He can help the sick person with them, but he can also kill him with them. For just as he can administer Lemon Balm <note>original: *Melissen*; Melissa officinalis, an herb traditionally used for heart health and calming the spirits.</note> for health, he can also administer arsenic for death. How is this to be understood? It is simply this: that we humans can work good or evil against one another through the power of our faith—provided that the Lord allows His carpenter <note>Paracelsus uses "carpenter" (Zimmermann) here as a metaphor for the divine or natural forces that carry out a person's inner intent.</note> to have his way.

[A] Thus our faith is nothing other than a craftsman's instrument. This same craftsman forges a knife so that he might strike his neighbor and injure <gloss>original: *letze*; to wound or damage</gloss> his body; without the knife or something similar, he cannot strike him. Understand this parable in the same way: if we wish to misuse faith and fall away from the purpose for which it was given to us, and direct the power of our faith down a false path, straying from the right one, and believe "this is that, that, and that"—this false misuse of the powers of our faith causes us to declare it so. It "forges the weapon" so that the thing we believe in becomes a reality. [A]

[A] Furthermore, know that this same "forged thing," which in physical terms is called a weapon, may well be called a **spirit** in this context. [A]

[A] For a spirit can do without hands or feet what a man does; therefore, if it produces the same effect, it is not unlike a man. [A]

[A] Now, to give a brief instruction concerning this "forging," for faith requires such an order: If we have a disease in the land and we conclude that it is a penance, a vengeance, or a plague <term>plague: here *Plag*, referring to a divinely permitted affliction rather than just a biological disease</term>, then so it becomes. And although the disease is natural in origin, faith makes it **unnatural**; it brings it to such a point that no one can recognize it by its natural signs anymore.

For if I were to describe and somewhat <term>temper</term> <note>original: *glimpffen*; to speak of something in a fitting, moderate, or appropriate way</note> the deeds of those sorcerers in their sorcery—what has happened through them by God’s permission—it would become a strange chronicle. To understand all these things briefly: faith makes the human being invisible; it forges and works that which the body would forge if it were able. For the human thus becomes a spirit, for whom such things are possible to accomplish.

And the strength of faith and of the body is not taken from us, unless it be through divine providence. In the same way that God might make a person sick—so that their physical strength and arrogance can do no harm to anyone, making them lame in hands and feet—He also lames the faith of such <term>wanton people</term> <note>original: *üppigen Leutt*; here referring to those who are arrogant, frivolous, or misuse their spiritual power</note>.

The same has happened with the **French Disease** <note>original: "Franzosen"; a common historical term for Syphilis.</note>: there they have concocted a connection to **Saint Dionysius** <note>Saint Dionysius (Denis) was often invoked against frenzy or headaches; Paracelsus is criticizing the practice of linking specific saints to specific diseases through superstition.</note> and the like, and have thus given birth to a "Dionysius" within their own faith, so that they are more incurable than curable.

<meta>This page continues Paracelsus’s argument from page 323, where he discussed how human imagination and "misguided faith" can manifest as physical disease. He previously used "Saint Vitus’s Dance" and the "French Disease" (Syphilis) as examples of how cultural beliefs and desperation can "poison" a person’s health. Here, he extends this critique to the religious sphere, specifically targeting the Anabaptist movement as a form of self-induced delusion.</meta>

<page-num>324</page-num>

In this way, other manifestations of faith are also devised which are similar to those already accepted—such as in **Saint Vitus’s Dance**—and these also arise from self-willed, formative heads <note>original: "plastigen Köpffen"; Paracelsus uses "plastic" in the sense of the mind’s power to "mold" or "shape" physical reality and disease.</note>:

These manifestations take their root in an envious heart and can allow nothing belonging to others to be held dear. They take for themselves a passage from the Scriptures and interpret it according to their own self-willed heads. And once they have "rhymed" <note>i.e., forced a logical or poetic connection</note> it according to their own minds, they invest such a powerful faith into it that the force of that very faith flows back into them, seizing and strengthening them so mightily that they will even stake their lives on their own understanding. This is demonstrated by the <term>Anabaptists</term> <note>original: "Wiedertauffer"; a radical Reformation movement. Paracelsus, a contemporary, is highly critical of them here, viewing their zeal as a psychological or medical delusion rather than true piety.</note>¹), who, through such misuse of a "mad faith," believe themselves into such a state that they die and perish in the manner they have prescribed for themselves. Indeed, their foundation and sect can have no other name, according to right understanding, than **Enchantment** <note>original: "Incantatio"</note>: ²) Not that they are bewitched by other people, but rather they drive themselves into a belief, so that by the power of that faith—and not by the truth—they commit themselves to the fire.

To better maintain this <note>the truth</note>, God has commanded no one to die for such a thing. He who wishes to die for the sake of His Word must be powerfully overflowing with the Holy Spirit; such a person dies blessedly. # BOOK TWO
## CONCERNING THE IMPRESSIONS OF THE HIDDEN HEAVENS, ENTIRELY MISSING
<note>original Latin: "LIBER SECUNDUS: DE IMPRESSIONIBUS COELI OCCULTI, TOTUS DESIDERATUR." This note indicates that a portion of the original manuscript or series was lost before this edition was printed.</note>

### THE THIRD BOOK
### Concerning the Invisible Works of the Highly Learned Master Theophrastus Paracelsus

**S**O that one thing follows another, and the completed work is laid down, there follows hereafter the third book concerning Invisible Things. And it is my intention here in this book to describe only the powers of the works of imagination, which belong only to women during the time they are pregnant, and likewise how these things attach to children and are perceived <note>The German "ersehen" here refers to the theory of "maternal impression," where what a pregnant woman imagines or sees was believed to physically mark the child</note>: also for men, what their imagination <gloss>1) imagination or fantasy [original Latin: *imaginatio*]</gloss> does to them. Now, although until now no one has touched upon this in the foundation of philosophy: I shall not be ashamed to be the first in this as well, as I was in the aforementioned previous books.

For the time of harvest gives to the necessary things, which have grown ripe for the harvest, its reaper and its wagoner, so that each thing may be brought to light in its own time.

<meta>Following the introduction to the Third Book, Paracelsus continues his metaphor of the "harvest" of knowledge, distinguishing between true philosophy and the superficial "chaff" of previous scholars, before moving into his specific study of the "invisible body."</meta>

Many have thought and imagined that they have harvested the wheat of philosophy: but it was a worthless grain, a husk without a kernel, empty chaff, or bran in which there was no flour. But how long does one labor at such a harvest, or who is fed by it? No one! For harvesting too early brings no bread into the house. However, when the harvest is truly here, things are handled according to the custom of the harvest time.

Therefore, reader, because the works of the imagination—those of women and also those of men—are wonderful, it is right to seek the origin of such things that the invisible body <note>original: "Cörpel." Paracelsus uses this term to describe the "astral" or "sidereal" body, which he believed governed human health, emotions, and the power of the mind independently of the physical flesh.</note> handles and transforms among us. In order that no sorcery, hauntings, or ghostly dealings might be found herein, nor attributed to superstitious sects, I wish to describe the foundation of these things. I shall not avail myself of any authority from the old writers; rather, disregarding them all, I will show the demonstration of the Light of Man <note>A Paracelsian term for natural reason and divine insight granted to humanity to understand the world.</note>, wherein you may remember that this is the true foundation and no other. In this way, reader, you may know how to conduct yourself.

## Introduction to the Third Book

**S**INCE everything has now been sufficiently revealed in the first preface—namely, that man is composed of two parts, the visible and the invisible—it is not my intention to write about the visible part, unless it happens that it must serve as a parable. For what is more appropriate to present as a parable than things that are alike? But I will write further concerning the invisible body, and regarding this, take note first of this example. The visible body has its effect in all things, and all its movement and what it does is seen by man. Now, however, that which is seen is only half the work: the other half of the work no one sees, for it is done by the invisible body. Just as a carpenter, who...

Now, no art is given by God unless it also possesses the necessities for its completion. So, note this example and what purpose it serves.

**Imagination** is a master craftsman <note>original: "Werckmeiſter." It is so subtle and powerful that it is possible for it to imitate everything the eyes see and comprehend, even if its own visible body cannot do so.

So sharp and ingenious is this art <term>Kunſt</term> <note>Here "Kunſt" refers to both a learned skill and an innate spiritual capacity or "virtue."</note> that it paints a fly off a wall onto the ground it possesses; and as sharply as the eyes can observe, it is possible for it to design a spiderweb just as sharply as the eyes and the spiders can see and make it.

Since the building is done upon the earth, it is shown by the construction itself that the child is the "earth." Thus, the structures of the imagination prove which part is the earth in the mother's womb: it is found that the works and buildings stand upon the child. Therefore, the child is the earth, and that in which it lies is the outer sphere and orbs, which we call the **heavens**.

# Paracelsus, Paramirum
## 22

Every external thing has two bodies, the visible and the invisible, and so each body takes what belongs to it. Just as much is taken by the body when the **exalted formation** <note>original: "exaltirte Bildung." In alchemy, "exaltation" refers to raising a substance to a higher state of purity or power; here it refers to the spiritual or formative blueprint of a thing.</note> does not accompany it, so too is much taken from the **exalted formation** when the **exalted body** <note>original: "exaltirt Corpus."</note> does not accompany it.

Now, observe a further example. It is said: **"It is raining frogs."** Pay attention to how this occurs. The things that create the rain are the **invisible bodies** of humans. In the same way, the Earth is the visible body. Now, frogs are earthly and spring from the Earth, which is where the visible body takes its origin. Now, the fact that it rains frogs is "against nature," for the reason that they grow from the Earth and not from the rain. However, the fact that they *do* come from the rain means they emerge from the **invisible body**, which stands alongside the Earth in an equal state of **generation** <note>original: "Generation." The process of being born or produced.</note>. Therefore, the frogs of the Earth are visible in their foundation and origin, while the others are invisible. This happens in this way: the upper body <note>The Heavens or the spiritual/invisible realm.</note> has the **attracting power** <note>original: "anziehend Krafft."</note> to take things from the Earth into itself; the Earth also has the **attracting power** to pull things from the upper realm into itself.

The Earth pulls something invisible to itself and makes it visible at night; the Heavens pull something visible out of the Earth and make it invisible. And when each returns to the place from which it came, it appears before the eyes just as it was before. Now, the Sun attracts to itself whatever is commanded by its **magnet** <note>original: "Magneten." Paracelsus believed celestial bodies acted like magnets, drawing up "essences" from the Earth to be processed in the heavens.</note>, and so does every star according to its magnetic nature. In this way, the "frog-essence" is also drawn upward through the **pregnant nature** <note>original: "ſchwanger Art."</note> of the Heavens. And just as a **birthmark** <note>original: "Muttermal." Literally "mother-mark." It was believed that a mother's strong desires or fears could "mark" the skin of the unborn child.</note> appears on a child, so too is the birth of these frogs. For the **imaginative power** <note>original: "einbildete Krafft." This is the core concept of the "Paramirum": the power of the mind or the stars to give form to matter.</note> resides in Heaven, and the Earth is the child; that which falls upon the Earth from Heaven is that which the star has envisioned within itself, and according to...

<summary>Paracelsus explains the phenomenon of "raining frogs" as a result of the magnetic attraction between the visible Earth and the invisible Heavens, comparing it to how a mother's imagination creates birthmarks on a child.</summary>

So too may a deceiver in medicine arise, and say of such medicine, "Nature does not do it, **Asmatheus** <note>likely a reference to the demon Asmodeus; Paracelsus argues that what people mistake for demonic activity is often just an "invisible" but natural force</note> does it." And he may well maintain and protect this [view], for the sophistical physicians allow this out of their lack of understanding. 

Therefore, reader, great are the virtues of nature; who is so thirsty that he dares to claim for himself so many of her powers, as many as are within her? For these powers all proceed from divine wisdom. Who can come to an end of wisdom, while the Scripture says it is without number, and speaks of the great height and incomprehensibility of His wisdom? What then shall man in the depths of the earth propose and think for himself, even when he gazes at the highest point in the **Light of Nature** <term>Licht der Natur: For Paracelsus, this is the innate knowledge of the world and medicine that God allows humans to discover through observation and experience, distinct from the light of grace or revelation</term>, as to how he stands against the wisdom of God? It is no different than the distance from the ground of the earth up through the sun, and even further through the new sun, which will be seven times clearer; even then, he has not yet reached the beginning of Divine Wisdom. But because the Light of Nature is like the **crumbs from the Lord's table** <note>A reference to Matthew 15:27; Paracelsus suggests that even "pagans" can access truth through nature</note>, to be accepted by all heathens, and the Light of Nature has departed from **Judah** <note>Here used metaphorically to refer to the established religious or intellectual elite who have lost sight of natural truth</note>, it is not fitting to let it go, but rather to gather up wisdom as long as a tiny crumb falls.

Although this same thing is too high for us to fully fathom: therefore let praise, honor, and glory be said to the kind, eternal God, who lets the Light of Nature shine upon us, so that we may know how to walk thoroughly within natural powers.

<meta>This page continues the author’s exploration of the distinction between the physical corpse and the spiritual saint. Having previously warned against the veneration of graves, he now explains the process of "glorification"—the transformation of the earthly body into a heavenly state—and argues that while on earth, true holiness is often indistinguishable from natural phenomena without the testimony of Christ.</meta>

<page-num>363</page-num>
<sig>A</sig>

Once the **body** <note>original: "Cörper"</note> is in the earth, the saint is in Heaven. Therefore, whatever lies in the earth and whatever it performs is natural; likewise, whatever is in Heaven and whatever it performs is supernatural. Now, understood in this way, the saint shall rise again on the **Last Day** <note>The Day of Judgment</note> and give an account of his life in his body: so know that this same body must be glorified. What is the **glorification** of the body other than the taking away of its natural powers? How is a saint distinguished from me or others, except only in that he is glorified? That is, he has nothing natural left about him, whereas I am stuck full of nature. For if a saint were to be a saint and yet still possess natural powers within him, who could distinguish the works of the saint from the works of nature? For the power of nature is so wonderful that it may well be recognized as "holy" by the common people. 

It is a hard thing to speak of and rough to look upon—a saint who walks upon the earth and is not yet separated from natural powers, and he performs signs. One wonders: does nature do this, or does **holiness**? Unless it were the case that he confirmed his works in the name of **Jesus**. Who else would consider his treading on water <note>The author uses "Wasser tretten," likely referring to the miracle of walking on water as a test of genuine sanctity versus natural trickery</note> to be the work of a saint? The peasants are easily persuaded; but for me, it is quite difficult while still here on earth. Who is glorified? He whom death has overlooked? And could anyone be glorified if they were not first a mortal beginner? And whatever is not glorified, should we acknowledge it as anything but a natural creature? 

Whatever clings to the **lump of clay** <note>original: "Leimenklotzen," a derogatory or humble term for the physical, material body</note> must pass away: therefore the **elements** shall dissolve, and everything that grows from them. When these things dissolve, what would the nature of the body do, which comes from the elements? All things shall be glorified: where then will the bodies and their earthly attachments go? Regarding natural <term>Arcana</term> <note>In this context, hidden natural secrets or inner medicinal/magical virtues</note>, these pass away in the process of glorification. And before glorification, no one knows who anyone truly is, unless the testimony of **Christ** is at hand.

Although these are stinking carrion, I take it upon myself to describe natural things herein. $^1$) Scraps [diminutive of *pars*, meaning "part" or "piece"] = little pieces; Scrap-sack = the bread bag of schoolchildren. Thomas Platter’s [1544–1578] autobiography tells us with exceptionally fresh color of this student life. What if that were the full form for that *Schütz*? A well-known student expression for a beginning student [Fresh... fox <note>original: "Sch...fuchs"; a reference to the term "Schißfuchs" or "freshman," implying someone who is still "shitting" their fox-fur</note>] offers itself as an explanation and as a hint to the region where one has to look for etymologies. — Friedrich Paulsen, *History of Learned Instruction in German Schools and Universities*. Leipzig 1896. Vol. I, p. 20.

1) This is an ancient Germanic concept. We encounter it as early as the *Nibelungenlied* when Hagen steps before the body of Siegfried. Amos Comenius <note>Jan Amos Comenius (1592–1670), a famous Czech philosopher and educator</note>, who was so extensively influenced by Paracelsus, discusses this question at length in Chapter X [On Animals] of his *Physica* [1633]. Hence it comes that when he approaches the corpse—especially when he also touches or looks at it—all that is still present of the spirit in the corpse rushes with its vehicle, the blood, toward that which meets its spirit, namely through *sympathy*. But this *necromancy*, a standard or even a flying banner moved by the wind, is the leader of the stupid crowd, which with its barking constantly bears witness to the infinite effects of such art; and books are filled, affirming that spirits acted and could speak without a tongue, and without the organic instruments without which one cannot speak, and spoke, and carried extremely heavy loads, caused storms and rain, and that humans turned into cats, into wolves and other beasts, although those who claim such things are the first to enter into beasts."

# The Fifth Book

## On the Invisible Works of the Highly Learned Lord Theophrastus von Hohenheim, Doctor <note>Theophrastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541) is the birth name of the famous physician and alchemist known as Paracelsus.</note>

### Preface to the Reader

AND if I should perhaps please those many <term>sects</term> <note>original: *Secten*; Paracelsus frequently used this term to disparage rival academic, medical, or religious factions that he believed lacked practical experience.</note> here which have grown out of their own heads, who have no experience in wisdom, and who do not pursue the foundation of truth—even though they make a great show of themselves, there is no power in it. For what can be built upon their fickle hearts, which are always set upon vain and future schemes, and whose praise and blame please only their own kind? For where does the <term>reed</term> <note>A biblical and proverbial metaphor for someone who is unstable and easily swayed by the "winds" of opinion or trend.</note> stand, except in the place where the wind can strike it? Such frivolity breaks out daily with innovations, through which they wish to win praise for themselves; they desire to possess that which they do not actually strive for, and they keep company with the blind so that their squinting and one-eyed sight might have some appearance of authority.

I, however, continue to write about <term>characters</term> <note>original: *Characteren*; in Paracelsian thought, these are spiritual symbols, sigils, or astrological signs believed to have the power to influence the human body and soul.</note>, and how these same things work within us human beings. Not that I wish to forge work for the "shouters in the chambers" <note>original: *Schreyern auff den Stuben*; a derogatory reference to university scholars or armchair theorists who argue loudly in their rooms but have no practical knowledge of nature.</note>; but rather for you, the learned and experienced, so that those things which have been extravagantly interpreted might be recognized, and it may be seen how unfairly he [is dealt with]... <note>The sentence is interrupted by the page break; the original German "ge-" likely continues as "gehandelt" or "geschehen" on the following page.</note>

Therefore, the power of names and words, spoken or written—in whatever way that occurs—is my intention to describe: also to instruct here, what should be attributed to or taken away from things. Therefore, Reader, do not judge unless you have experienced the good foundation.

Who can be an enemy to a woman, let her be as she will? And although fire is our enemy, hates us and everything that enters it, and desires to swallow and consume it all, we are the ones who have power over the fire and it is under our hands; therefore, good comes to us out of the fire. We should not enjoy the hostility of the fire, but rather the fact that we have the power to compel it to do us good; and we should enjoy that same benefit, and thank God for it.

For from this it follows that we are called and compelled toward an **affect**, one in this, another in that. Now, upon this, the command is carried out through the angel or spirit. Now we have the power to learn that which we desire. And just as the **Salutation** <note>original: *Gruß*; referring again to the Angelic Salutation to Mary mentioned on the previous page</note> was given to Mary, after which she was full of grace, so too are the graces distributed among us.

And everything that we discover takes its origin in this way. Therefore, no one should allow themselves to be troubled by the **means** <note>original: *Mittel*; the intermediaries, such as spirits or angels, through which knowledge reaches humans</note> through which such things reach us. Instead, we should have hope that whether it comes through an evil or a good spirit, they do all these things by the command of God. For God wills that everything be obedient to Him, and that we see and perceive His power and might—in Hell just as well as in Heaven—and He wills that those things which are in Heaven and Hell serve us, His chosen ones.

Since both evil and good spirits are all **creatures** <note>original: *Creaturen*; in this context, "created beings" who are entirely subject to the Creator</note>, then the things they are capable of are also "created." Thus, they have nothing of their own, but everything that exists is from God. How then can anyone say that he learns from the Devil? Since the Devil is not a God? Thus, everyone must confess that not a single bird would fly upon the earth if God did not send it, nor a single nettle grow if it were not God’s command. If it did not please God that we should have these things, He would not allow them to be granted to us. Since He allows them to be granted, we must surely judge that God does not mean us any harm by them, but intends them for our good and out of divine faithfulness.

What then is evil in these **arts** <note>original: *Künsten*; refers to any specialized knowledge, craft, or science, including those we might now call "occult"</note>? Nothing, except for that which we ourselves make evil. Prayer and fasting are good, for they "drive out the devils." Knocking and ringing [of bells] are also good. Thus, all these things are good and permitted—even commanded—for us to use for our benefit. But it is not good if we practice prayer and fasting like the <term>Tetrici</term> <note>original: *Tetrici*; a Latin term for those who are gloomy, harsh, or severe. Paracelsus uses it here to describe hypocrites who perform religious acts with a false, somber outward show of piety</note>. That is to say: we should wash our faces so that we appear to know nothing of our fasting, so that it is the heart, and not just the mouth, that is moved. Now...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that all knowledge and "arts" are divine gifts mediated by spirits, asserting that since spirits are merely God's creatures, their influence is part of a providential plan. He concludes that the morality of such knowledge depends on the user's sincere intent rather than the spiritual intermediary.</summary>

<keywords>divine providence, spirits, origin of knowledge, nature of evil, prayer and fasting, Tetrici, hypocrisy, Paracelsus</keywords>

--- Page 413 ---
<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous section regarding the direct relationship between God and the individual. Paracelsus shifts focus to the role of "ceremonies" or outward rituals, arguing that they often act as unnecessary or even idolatrous barriers to the grace that God provides freely to the heart.</meta>

<page-num>393</page-num>

It follows from this that for some, fasting and prayer serve for harm. Not that fasting and prayer are evil in themselves; but what is added to them is evil. Know this: since God now allows gifts to fall upon us through such a **Salutation** <note>original: *Gruß*; referencing the divine message or "fullness of grace" like that given to Mary</note>, according to each person's **calling** <note>original: *Beruff*; the specific vocation or station in life God has assigned to an individual</note>—for we take this calling upon ourselves—we should not handle these gifts in a <term>tetrisch</term> <note>an archaic term used by Paracelsus meaning difficult, pompous, or unnecessarily complicated</note> manner.

That is to say, we require no **ceremonies** for this. <margin>These words reveal a mindset that is entirely outside the established Church and yet remains foreign to the various religious sects of the time.</margin> For it would be a deception if we sought to obtain such things, or had already obtained them, and yet did not wish to go from ourselves directly to God without **intermediaries** <note>original: *oh Mittel*; without secondary agents, rituals, or "middlemen" between the soul and God</note>. Instead, our affairs are now overwhelmed by ceremonies through which God has never commanded us to seek Him. And again, if God has sent us the Salutation of grace, and we then tried to maintain that same grace through ceremonies, we would be very close to **idolatry**.

In all these matters, **Mary** should serve as our example; she was full of grace, yet no ceremony was used either before or after. We should walk in those same footsteps, for she did not go astray. Therefore, we also will not go astray if we follow her path. But every other way is a wandering in error.

Now, regarding these ceremonies, I am inclined to tell you of their "power." This is not only because it serves my current purpose, but also for a broader reason: namely, that God desires the heart alone, and not ceremonies. He also requires that, since our heart has received from Him, we should distribute that same grace from our hearts to others. For whatever we receive from God, we receive freely; and in that same way, it should be given out again. If we were to stain it with ceremonies, we would fall into **pride**, which is not pleasing to God.

Regarding these ceremonies, I want it understood that all such rituals are similar; they are the reason why the term **idolatry** may rightly be used in this context.

<summary>Paracelsus argues that religious ceremonies are unnecessary and potentially idolatrous, as God's grace is a direct gift to the heart that should be shared freely without ritualistic complications. He presents Mary as the ideal model of receiving grace without the need for outward religious forms.</summary>
<keywords>ceremonies, grace, Mary, idolatry, calling, prayer, fasting, pride, direct relationship with God</keywords>

...be. And I will therefore instruct you with such examples. We have our order and teaching from **Christ** <note>original: *Christo*</note>, and namely, we have no power to add to it or take away from it; this applies to every single person. ¶

¶ For every human being is his own closest neighbor before God; and has full power to settle his affairs with God. If, however, a person is the one who gives such power out of his hand, and does not keep what God has given him, but entrusts it to another and seeks Him through that person: now he falls into ceremonies and clings to despair. For every ceremony is the **winepress** <note>original: *Trotten*; a term for a winepress or a place where grapes are trodden. Paracelsus uses this to suggest that ceremonies are a mechanism of despair that "treads upon" or crushes the spirit.</note> of despair. Now it follows from this: because such power is given out of one’s hand, faith and all its powers are also given out of one's hand; and in the very place to which it is given, ceremonies arise. These ceremonies are merely an outward appearance given to the things that have been entrusted there. For he who gives faith out of his hand is robbed of his faith, and the one to whom he gave it now possesses it. ¶

¶ As much as he now has to distribute from it, so much he pays. This payment rests with God; it is worth as much as His divine will dictates. Whether it be evil or good also rests with His divine will. He will look upon the heart in these matters. ¶

¶ Now, however, so that I may make an end of ceremonies, know that they simply should not exist. For if we are to acquire anything from God, He looks at the heart and not the ceremony. If He has given us something, He also does not want us to consume it in ceremonies, but rather through our labor. For He gives nothing else but that through which we love God from our hearts, with our strength...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that individuals possess a direct, God-given power to manage their own spiritual affairs, and that delegating this agency to religious rituals is a surrender of faith. He portrays ceremonies as "winepresses of despair" that provide only an outward appearance of piety while robbing the individual of true spiritual strength.</summary>

<keywords>spiritual agency, direct relationship with God, ceremonies, ritualism, faith, despair, winepress metaphor, spiritual labor, the heart</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the critique of religious and magical mediation. While the previous page argued that ceremonies lead to despair and the loss of personal faith, this page explains how Satan uses these rituals to corrupt the "Magical Art" and distract from the power of the heart.</meta>

...and with a whole spirit, so that we may help our neighbor. When it serves this purpose—that He gives to us—then all **ceremonies** are forgotten. In this way, ceremonies have crept into all things and corrupted the **Magical Art** <term>Magical Art (original: *Kunſt Magica*); in this context, it refers to the natural and spiritual power humans possess through God, rather than sorcery</term>. What I am writing about now has come to the point where nothing is supposed to work without ceremonies. For in the same way that we act toward God without opening our hearts, we are also expected to act here in this art; yet we are all equally powerful, one as much as the other. ❦

❦ Now, however, to prevent this power from acting on its own, it has been arranged—with **Satan** as the instigator—that we should not use such powers unless ceremonies precede them. What, then, are the ceremonies of these arts? Hypocritical fasting and prayer: just as the **Pharisees** <note>In the New Testament, the Pharisees are often depicted as prioritizing outward ritual over inner piety; Paracelsus uses them here as a symbol of religious hypocrisy.</note> put on a display before the people, so too must the Pharisaic way be used here for the Devil—with specific numbers, specific times, and various forms of abstinence, with many blessings and benedictions, with holy water, and the like. Thus has the Devil taken it into his hands; whoever wishes to obtain something from God in this manner must forget God and use these ceremonies, believing that the result happens because of them. Now, let **Theology** judge how these things are to be measured: for just as men live and walk among one another in the deception of their own power, so it is also with the aforementioned spirits. ❦

❦ It is not that I wish to speak against the **authority of Peter** <note>original: *Petro in ſein Gewalt*; a reference to the "Power of the Keys" or the institutional authority of the Pope and the Church.</note>, but I want to state that everyone should have a tranquil heart within themselves. The reason I say this is because the **characters** <term>characters (original: *Character*); these are symbolic sigils or marks used in Renaissance magic to represent spiritual forces</term> are not words, nor are they names. But the ceremonialists have turned them into words and names so that the spirits would be regarded through them—as if the spirit would do nothing if it were not called upon. This is the same as if one did not give "good words" to Peter, then...

<summary>Paracelsus argues that the "Magical Art" has been corrupted by the Devil through the introduction of ceremonies, such as ritual fasting and holy water, which distract from the innate power of a quiet heart. He asserts that magical symbols (characters) have been wrongly treated as names or words used to command spirits rather than as reflections of internal spiritual power.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the fifth book of the Paramirum. Having previously discussed the "invisible body" and the deceptive nature of magical signs, Paracelsus now warns against spiritual pride and the "subtle" deceptions of spirits that lead to the formation of religious sects.</meta>

# Paracelsus, Paramirum
## 26

...proceed by divine command and decree, and not by mere **providence** <note>original: *Verhängnuß*; referring to things God permits to happen rather than what He actively commands</note>. We must hold so firmly to the glory of God that we do not deviate from it in any matter, and thus protect ourselves. For spirits are teachers of the arts, but they often sneak in falsely under the appearance of a divine command, teaching very subtle things, sharp and lofty thoughts, great prestige in all arts, much chatter, and cleverness.

Thus, let those who wallow in sin and yet wish to be **Apostles** beware. They are easily led into that school. And those who place their own spirit before the Holy Spirit, their desire and longing is to break that which cannot be broken. See there their self-righteous heads in the sects, who maintain specific articles and make them significant, which the Apostles had left in simplicity: such as your **Anabaptists**¹), **Bohemians**²) and **Trinitarians**³)! With this, I wish to conclude the fifth book on what is to be understood regarding <term>Characters</term> <note>original: *Charactern*; magical signs, sigils, or symbols believed to hold occult power</note>, which has been sufficiently presented.

---

¹) The well-known sect of the so-called **Anabaptists**; cf. what was said previously on p. 324. ²) **Bohemian Brethren**. This community of conviction—emerging from the Taborite movement of the **Hussite Wars**—was formed in 1457 in Kunwald near Senftenberg as the Bohemian Brethren's Unity by Gregor, a nephew of Rokitzana. But already around 1420, Peter of Chelčic had expressed their early Christian ideals. In 1450, these were represented by the so-called "Chelčic Brethren," who then transformed into the "Bohemian Brethren." ³) **Trinitarians**. The Catholic "Order of the Most Holy Trinity," which was founded by the Parisian theologian John of Matha and the hermit Felix of Valois in the year 1198. Pope Innocent III approved it. The purpose of the order at that time was the ransoming of captive Christians from the **Saracens** <note>a medieval term for Muslims</note>. — It is interesting how Paracelsus brings these three names together. This offers us again a proof of his completely non-denominational and sect-free religion. Admittedly, however, it exhibits nuances that are to be found precisely among the morally great of the Anabaptists and Bohemian Brethren.

**Parts 1 and 2: On the causes and origin of diseases from the three primary substances** <note>original Latin: *De causis et origine morborum ex tribus primis substantiis*; referring to Paracelsus’s "tria prima": Salt, Sulfur, and Mercury</note> . . . . . . { **83—129** and **130—172**
**Part 3: On the causes and origin of diseases from <term>Tartar</term>** <note>original Latin: *De causis et origine morborum ex Tartaro*; Tartar refers to stony or calcified deposits in the body, such as kidney stones or gouty crystals, which Paracelsus compared to the sediment in wine casks</note> . . . **173—232**
**Part 4: On the cause and origin of diseases of the <term>Womb</term>** <note>original Latin: *De causa et origine morborum Matricis*; the "Matrix" was the Paracelsian term for the female reproductive system and the unique medical needs of women</note> . . . **233—290**
**Part 5: On the cause and origin of <term>invisible diseases</term>** <note>original Latin: *De causa et origine morborum invisibilium*; these are diseases of the spirit, mind, or those caused by non-physical influences</note> . . . **291—401**
